title: When Forms Become Law: Constituent-Facing Information Systems as Vectors of Substantive Non-Compliance in Public Administration

detail.title: When Forms Become Law: Constituent-Facing Information Systems as Vectors of Substantive Non-Compliance in Public Administration
detail.abstract:
Public agencies increasingly rely on constituent-facing digital systems to implement statutory and regulatory programs. These systems are typically evaluated in terms of efficiency, modernization, and service delivery. This working paper argues that they should also be evaluated as quasi-regulatory instruments. Drawing on administrative burden theory, digital governance scholarship, and established usability research, the paper examines how routine design and validation decisions embedded in legacy public-sector systems can function as sources of substantive non-compliance.

Using a case study of a state unemployment insurance claimant portal, the analysis demonstrates how navigation inconsistency, accessibility deficiencies, and presumptive form dependencies can impede lawful compliance and narrow eligibility pathways beyond those authorized by statute or rule. The findings suggest that technical debt in constituent-facing systems constitutes governance debt, exposing public agencies to legal and political vulnerability even absent intentional policy change. The paper concludes by outlining governance strategies for aligning digital implementation with statutory intent while modernization efforts proceed.

The analysis employs a structured heuristic evaluation grounded in established usability principles and accessibility standards.

title: Health care team service capacity planning: A mixed-integer nonlinear programming approach
affiliations: School of Public Health, Texas A&M University, University of Florida and University of Florida

detail.title: Health care team service capacity planning: A mixed-integer nonlinear programming approach
detail.abstract: In the health care industry, services are delivered by multi-specialty teams, comprised of personnel with different, typically complementary, skill sets often associated with their scope of practice. In this paper, we develop a mixed-integer nonlinear programming model to determine the minimal cost service capacity plan for a health care facility that determines the number and composition of health care teams to provide service for its patients that achieve a desired level of service performance over a planning horizon. The service performance metric of interest is the timeliness of the service, quantified by the average time that a patient spends in the system. We apply our model to hospital-based and freestanding outpatient-based care centers, where there are two classes of patients with different priorities and server-type-dependent service times, and two types of teams and examination/treatment rooms with asymmetric substitutability and patient-class-dependent service rates that characterize each team’s scope of practice. We develop queueing models and approximation methods to compute the average time that a patient spends in the system for each patient class with sufficient accuracy. Using these results, we then use the capacity planning model to determine the minimal cost service capacity plan for the health care teams for the planning horizon. The performance of our approximation approach and the capacity planning model is assessed by a computational study. Our investigation shows that our approximation approach provides sufficiently accurate results that can be used in practice to make long-term health care team service capacity planning decisions.

title: Rare-Earth Exposure and Bottlenecks in AI Data Centers: Cost and Schedule Risk

detail.title: Rare-Earth Exposure and Bottlenecks in AI Data Centers: Cost and Schedule Risk

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
AI data centers (AIDCs) are often described as electricity-hungry assets. This study treats AI DCs as gigawatt-scale capital builds and focuses on how a small set of REE-bound subcomponents enter the campus cost stack yet exert outsized leverage on delivery timelines. Generic criticality rankings and sector-level demand narratives rarely locate this dependence inside the campus cost stack, where procurement decisions and lead times are actually managed.

An auditable bridge is developed from build economics to element-level exposure. A per-GW AI-campus CAPEX baseline is decomposed into a transparent taxonomy of buckets and subcomponents, then mapped to REE-bound components using documented physical mechanisms. Bounded cost-intensity parameters and a 0–2 schedule-at-risk score are used to discipline uncertainty and separate cost exposure from schedule vulnerability. These inputs are consolidated into a traceable Rare-earth Exposure (REX) metric and extended with forward-looking scenarios that jointly evolve CAPEX mix and intensity parameters under plausible architecture shifts and substitution pathways.

In the baseline (mid) case, total mapped exposure is ≈ US$158.0M/GW, concentrated in IT equipment (≈ US$149.2M/GW; 94.4%) with a smaller cooling contribution (≈ US$8.8M/GW; 5.6%). Servers and accelerators account for ≈ US$138.8M/GW (87.8%), dominated by Nd (≈ US$83.3M/GW) and Pr (≈ US$34.7M/GW), with heavy-REE add-ons (Dy ≈ US$16.7M/GW; Tb ≈ US$4.2M/GW). Normalized, Nd exposure is 17.49 bp of total CAPEX. Cost share and delivery risk need not align: schedule-weighted exposure can be driven by long-lead, qualification-sensitive components. Scenario results show that design evolution reallocates exposure across elements and channels, revealing both mitigating and amplifying pathways that static assessments miss.

title: Network Effects and Compatibility in Accounting Standards: A Literature Review and a Case Study

detail.title: Network Effects and Compatibility in Accounting Standards: A Literature Review and a Case Study

detail.abstract: This paper identifies unresolved issues surrounding the international convergence of accounting standards by reexamining existing accounting research from the perspective of network effects and compatibility in economics. The analysis shows that empirical studies on IFRS adoption implicitly assume the presence of indirect network effects. Considering the presence of indirect network effects, the coexistence of multiple standards in Japan may be explained by increasing compatibility among standards. This study also examines compatibility through a case analysis of a single company by comparing the similarity of financial figures and textual disclosures under Japanese GAAP and IFRS. We find that similarity in financial figures increased over time, and similarity in note disclosures increased in the most recent year. These findings point to the need for future research to develop frameworks that measure how compatibility between standards influences network effects.

title: From Strategic Diagnosis to Policy Implementation: The BAFI Matrix as an Instrument for Public Value-Oriented Management in Environmental Institutions

detail.title: From Strategic Diagnosis to Policy Implementation: The BAFI Matrix as an Instrument for Public Value-Oriented Management in Environmental Institutions
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the BAFI Matrix as a strategic implementation instrument for public organizations operating in complex policy environments. Drawing on theories of public value, innovation, strategic planning, and SWOT analysis, it argues that traditional diagnostic tools often fail to guide concrete implementation decisions. Through a qualitative case study of Chile's Agency for Sustainability and Climate Change, the article demonstrates how BAFI translates organizational diagnosis into actionable strategic priorities. The matrix identifies zones of strength, protection, constraint, and critical risk, enabling evidence-informed decision-making. The paper contributes a replicable methodological tool for strengthening implementation capacity in public environmental governance.

detail.abstract: Emerging markets exhibit complex and non-linear patterns of category evolution that are inadequately explained by traditional maturity and adoption models. Existing frameworks such as the Product Life Cycle and Diffusion of Innovation primarily emphasize temporal diffusion while neglecting structural, cultural, and socioeconomic constraints. This paper proposes AM³ (Applied Market Maturity Matrix), a multidimensional diagnostic framework designed to assess category maturity and growth readiness in emerging market contexts. AM³ integrates seven critical dimensions: market awareness, competition intensity, customer class penetration, migration readiness, cost and logistics efficiency, cultural fit, and consumer affordability. The study further introduces the Readiness Vector (RV) as a secondary analytical tool to identify latent growthenabling conditions within immature categories. The framework is designed for cross-sector applicability and is illustrated through multiple consumer and B2B product categories in emerging markets. Findings indicate that categories may exhibit substantial growth readiness despite low overall maturity, reflecting dimensional asymmetry in market development. The paper contributes to market evolution theory by conceptualizing maturity as a systems-based process and provides practitioners with a structured tool for market entry, localization, and scaling decisions in emerging economies.

title: IERSE: An Explainable Hybrid Eligibility and Risk Scoring Framework for Immigration Decision Support

detail.title: IERSE: An Explainable Hybrid Eligibility and Risk Scoring Framework for Immigration Decision Support

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing personal, professional, or financial interests that could have influenced the research presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants or real personal data. All evaluations were conducted using synthetically generated datasets designed to simulate realistic scenarios. As a result, formal ethics approval or informed consent was not required.

detail.abstract: Immigration adjudication is a complex, high-stakes process involving detailed eligibility criteria, extensive documentation, and multi-factor risk assessment. Human officers retain full decision authority, but manual preliminary evaluation is time-consuming and prone to inconsistencies. This paper introduces the Intelligent Eligibility and Risk Scoring Engine (IERSE), a humanin-the-loop, explainable decision-support framework combining rule-based eligibility evaluation with machine learning-based multi-dimensional risk scoring. IERSE processes structured and unstructured applicant data, applies deterministic eligibility rules, and generates interpretable risk indicators across fraud, compliance, identity, economic, and security dimensions. Simulation results on 10,000 synthetic profiles demonstrate the potential to reduce preliminary processing time by approximately 65% relative to fully manual preliminary screening, while achieving high consistency in eligibility evaluation (98%) and strong precision and recall for risk signal identification. The framework is explicitly designed to support officer judgment rather than automate adjudication, providing transparent, auditable outputs that assist case prioritization and review. IERSE illustrates how hybrid, explainable AI architectures can improve efficiency, consistency, and transparency in high-stakes public-sector decision-support workflows while preserving human authority.

title: Post-Experiment Decisions: The Dual Adjustments for Rollout and Downstream Optimizations *
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics, The University of Hong Kong and The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics

detail.title: Post-Experiment Decisions: The Dual Adjustments for Rollout and Downstream Optimizations *
detail.abstract: Firms increasingly use randomized experiments to decide whether to scale up an intervention and, if so, how to re-optimize related operational choices such as inventory, capacity, or pricing. In many settings, experiments are performed on small samples, so the estimated effect of the intervention is uncertain. A common practice is to plug a "significant" estimate of the effect into both (i) the rollout rule and (ii) the downstream optimization. However, this can lead to avoidable losses because the costs of over-versus underestimating the effect are often asymmetric. The technically ideal approach is to obtain a data-dependent decision rule that minimizes the Bayes risk, but this lacks transparency and requires more computations. We propose Predict-Adjust-Then-Rollout-Optimize (PATRO), a plug-in approach that keeps the standard estimate, but makes data-independent adjustments, respectively, for the two types of decision. We show that the two adjustments can be substitutes or complements and provide an alternating-iteration method to compute the pair. Surprisingly, PATRO performs both in theory and numerically close or equivalent to the Bayes-optimal benchmark, making it a simple, effective way to convert noisy experimental results into better rollout and operational decisions without changing a firm's estimation pipeline or decision models.

title: Strategic Promotion and Rating Dynamics in Service Systems
affiliations: Nanjing University - School of Management and Engineering, Nanjing University - School of Management and Engineering, City University of Hong Kong and Hong Kong Polytechnic University

detail.title: Strategic Promotion and Rating Dynamics in Service Systems
detail.abstract:
Problem definition: Online ratings play a central role in shaping customer expectations and guiding firm behavior. Departing from existing studies that largely focus on pricing decisions in goods markets, we investigate how promotion decisions interact with rating dynamics in congested service systems. 

Methodology: We develop a two-period queueing model in which a monopolistic service provider with privately known quality serves sequentially arriving customers who are heterogeneous in delay sensitivity. 

Results: Our analysis reveals that the optimal promotion strategy acts as a strategic substitute to service quality when the sensitivity of the rating system to incoming reviews is low, but becomes a strategic complement for the high-quality service when rating sensitivity is high. Notably, a low-quality firm facing high rating sensitivity optimally adopts a myopic promotion strategy that extracts short-term profit before exiting the market.  Counterintuitively, we find that higher rating sensitivity does not necessarily improve profitability. Specifically, higher rating sensitivity benefits the high-quality or low-capacity firm, but penalizes the low-quality or high-capacity firm, while the firm with intermediate attributes may exhibit a U-shaped profitability pattern.  We further demonstrate a fundamental misalignment between profit and welfare maximization. While a profit-maximizing firm may adopt aggressive strategies that lead to market collapse, the welfare-optimal policy moderates promotion to sustain long-term demand. Finally, we uncover a transparency paradox: intermediate rating sensitivity can align private profit incentives with social optimum for low-quality services, whereas excessive rating sensitivity may exacerbate inefficiency for high-quality services. 

Managerial implications: Our findings generate actionable implications for service providers, platform operators, and policymakers regarding promotion strategies, rating system design, and service market regulation.

title: Charging the Elephant in the Room: EV Incentives, Market Power, and Externalities

detail.abstract: We investigate the effectiveness of various tax instruments in correcting the environmental externalities (CO2 emissions, accidents, local and non-exhaust pollutants) in the Norwegian car market. Utilizing a model of household decisions on vehicle purchase and kilometers driven, we find that vehicle demand is highly responsive to price, with an estimated price elasticity of -3.8. Driving behavior is less sensitive to per-kilometer costs, with estimated elasticities ranging between -0.4 and -0.5. A central finding of the study is the critical role of market power; multi-product manufacturers set sizable markups (≈ 30%) that significantly exceed social marginal costs and curtail new-car sales. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that accounting for driving heterogeneity and spatial heterogeneity is essential for addressing distributional concerns in policy design. While Norway's current regime of high registration taxes and broad electric vehicle (EV) exemptions successfully drove adoption, there seems to be a road for improvement; it performs worse than a no-tax benchmark due to fiscal costs and distorted allocations. Additionally, while weight-based taxes can target non-exhaust emissions, the engine type remains the primary driver of external costs, and corrective measures must be carefully balanced against existing market power distortions.

title: The Financing Burden Channel: How Out-of-Pocket Health Payments Attenuate Productivity Returns

detail.title: The Financing Burden Channel: How Out-of-Pocket Health Payments Attenuate Productivity Returns

Analyses relied on anonymized microdata and did not involve any direct contact with human subjects; under Johns Hopkins University policies, this constitutes non-human subjects research and was therefore exempt from ethics review.

detail.abstract: Grossman's (1972) health capital model and Lucas's (1988) growth framework predict productive health investment under frictionless financing. We identify a financing burden channel violating this assumption: out-of-pocket (OOP) health payments attenuate productivity returns. Using fourteen years of Nigerian panel data (2010–2024) and instrumental variables estimation robust across seven estimators, we find financing burden reduces health's productivity by 56 percent at mean OOP and fully neutralizes it at 11.2 percent of income—statistically indistinguishable from WHO's 10 percent catastrophic threshold (p= 0.76). Approximately 14 percent of households exceed this threshold. Threshold breaches reduce income growth by 26 percent; high-OOP households exhibit double the vulnerability to rainfall shocks. Capping OOP at the threshold would restore positive health returns for 5.5 million households, disproportionately benefiting poor and rural populations and unlocking health-driven growth currently suppressed by financing frictions.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces a Cognitive Policy Engine (CPE) that utilizes advanced AI technologies to automatically read and analyze social program policies (e.g., SNAP, Medicaid) and generate structured eligibility rules. These rules are used for the automated evaluation of applicants and officer-assisted decision support. By leveraging cloud-based NLP services, the CPE performs entity extraction and dependency parsing to convert policy text into machine-readable JSON format. This enables the seamless evaluation of applicant eligibility and provides humanreadable, explainable outputs for program officers. A proof-of-concept demonstrates the feasibility of this system on multiple policies, generating structured rules and delivering actionable insights that improve efficiency and transparency in decision-making. The proposed framework demonstrates how AI-driven policy-to-rule transformation can be operationalized responsibly for large-scale public benefit administration with human-in-the-loop governance.

title: Measuring Organizational Capital: A Cross-Language, Cross-Platform Framework
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: Measuring Organizational Capital: A Cross-Language, Cross-Platform Framework
detail.abstract: Organizational capital is viewed as a key driver of persistent performance differences across firms, but measurement has been largely confined to English-language settings. We construct firm-year measures of organizational capital for Japan using employee reviews from a leading Japanese employee review platform. Closely following the prior work based on Glassdoor employee reviews, we develop a language-and platform-free measurement method and apply it to more than 600,000 Japanese-written employee reviews. The resulting measures are slow-moving, vary meaningfully across firms and CEOs, and positively predict profitability and market valuation, with modest movements around CEO turnover, consistent with the theory. We also build alternative measures using Japanese-specific pre-processing and find substantial agreement with our main measures. These results show that review-based measurement of organizational capital extends to non-English platforms and that our pipeline supports crosslanguage and cross-platform comparability.

title: Why Do Cartels Recur? A Structural Perspective on Enforcement and Market Incentives

detail.title: Why Do Cartels Recur? A Structural Perspective on Enforcement and Market Incentives
detail.abstract: This article examines why cartel conduct frequently recurs in concentrated markets despite increasingly severe sanctions and sophisticated antitrust enforcement regimes. While conventional deterrence models predict that higher fines and detection probabilities should eliminate collusion, empirical evidence points to repeated cycles of cartel disruption and reformation. The article advances a dynamic interpretation of cartel recurrence, arguing that enforcement often operates as a temporary shock rather than a permanent constraint on firms' incentives. In markets characterised by high concentration, repeated interaction, stable demand, entry barriers, and transparency, the economic incentives supporting coordination are continuously regenerated. Enforcement tools such as fines and leniency programmes effectively destabilise cartels in the short run, but their deterrent impact weakens when enforcement intensity is perceived as episodic. By framing enforcement as a time-varying parameter within a repeated strategic environment, the analysis clarifies why cartel recurrence should be understood as an equilibrium outcome rather than as evidence of weak enforcement. The article concludes by discussing implications for enforcement design, highlighting the importance of enforcement persistence and structural awareness for achieving durable deterrence.

title: Structural Competition Risks Observed in M&A Transactions: An Applied Perspective from Financial Practice

detail.title: Structural Competition Risks Observed in M&A Transactions: An Applied Perspective from Financial Practice
detail.abstract: Mergers and acquisitions have become a central mechanism through which market concentration evolves across multiple sectors, often with long-term competitive effects that extend beyond the scope of formal antitrust review. While merger control frameworks focus primarily on ex ante assessments of market structure and potential efficiencies, less attention has been given to the structural incentives embedded in transactional practice that shape post-merger competitive outcomes. Drawing on observations from financial and transactional practice, this paper identifies recurring structural risks associated with M&A activity that may undermine effective competition even when transactions comply with existing regulatory standards. The analysis highlights how deal structuring, valuation incentives, anticipated remedies, and strategic consolidation dynamics can interact in ways that reinforce market concentration over time. Rather than examining specific transactions, the paper adopts an applied and generalized perspective, focusing on patterns commonly observed in M&A processes across concentrated markets. These observations are then used to assess potential gaps between formal merger review and real-world competitive dynamics. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these structural risks for competition enforcement and policy design, emphasizing the importance of incorporating insights from transactional practice into antitrust analysis. By bridging financial practice and competition policy, the study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of how M&A activity can influence market structure and long-term competitive outcomes.

title: Regularisation as Structural Stabiliser in Convex Trajectory Optimisation

detail.title: Regularisation as Structural Stabiliser in Convex Trajectory Optimisation
detail.abstract: We study the stability of convex trajectory optimisation problems under stochastic parameter estimation error. Using a constrained multi period allocation framework with monotonicity constraints, we introduce a variance based stability metric and evaluate the impact of quadratic smoothness regularisation. Through Monte Carlo perturbation experiments across multiple regimes, we observe a 40 to 65 percent reduction in trajectory variance as the regularisation weight increases. The results suggest that temporal smoothness can function as a structural stabiliser that improves robustness without requiring full stochastic programming formulations. This work presents an experimental perspective on robustness in applied convex optimisation.

title: The Strategic Evolu on of Keppel Ltd. (1968-2026): A Complete Case Study of ICAI's Four Grand Corporate Strategies

detail.title: The Strategic Evolu on of Keppel Ltd. (1968-2026): A Complete Case Study of ICAI's Four Grand Corporate Strategies
detail.abstract: This case study analyses the Strategic Evolution of Keppel Ltd. (formerly Keppel Corporation) over five decades, adopting the Grand Strategy Framework: Stability, Expansion, Retrenchment, and Combination. This paper charts the journey of Keppel Ltd., which began as a government-backed shipyard in 1968, transitioned through aggressive conglomerate diversification into banking and property in the 1990s, and pivoted via a combination strategy during the post-2014 oil crisis. Finally, it examines "Vision 2030," highlighting the firm’s successful transition from an offshore shipyard to the 23rd largest Infrastructure Manager in the world. This research paper states that Keppel serves as a definitive model for corporate agility and long-term value creation in the Asia-Pacific Region.

title: Audit Partners' Cultural Trust and Audit Outcomes

contentType.other: Journal of Accounting and Economics, Forthcoming

detail.abstract: Building on economic theories of cultural transmission, we examine how audit partners' cultural trust influences audit outcomes. Based on the "presumptive doubt" perspective of professional skepticism, we propose that audit partners from trusting cultures are more likely to rely on management's assertions, while still exercising a high degree of caution and not naively trusting management. Consistent with our prediction, we find that audit partners from trusting cultures commit fewer Type I errors when issuing going concern opinions, without significantly increasing Type II errors. The reduction in Type I errors is primarily found when audit partners normally tend to be more conservative, and it is attenuated when management is less trustworthy. At the same time, audit partners from trusting cultures are also associated with more within-GAAP earnings management, suggesting that increased trust entails a cost. Collectively, our findings offer new insights into how cultural trust affects the assurance of accounting information.

title: Strategic Financial Planning and Mergers & Acquisitions as Drivers of Capital Allocation Efficiency and Economic Growth

detail.title: Strategic Financial Planning and Mergers & Acquisitions as Drivers of Capital Allocation Efficiency and Economic Growth
detail.abstract: Strategic financial planning and mergers and acquisitions (M&A) play a critical role in capital allocation efficiency, corporate growth, and overall economic performance. In increasingly complex and regulated business environments, inadequate financial strategy and poorly structured transactions can lead to misallocation of resources, reduced productivity, and systemic financial risk. This paper examines how advanced financial planning frameworks, combined with disciplined M&A practices, contribute to sustainable corporate value creation and broader economic efficiency. Drawing from professional experience in corporate finance, FP&A, controllership, and M&A transactions within large organizations, this study proposes a practical financial framework integrating valuation modeling, budgeting discipline, performance indicators, and strategic decision-making. The analysis highlights how structured financial governance improves investment quality, supports long-term growth, and enhances organizational resilience. The findings demonstrate that robust financial strategy and well-executed M&A processes not only benefit individual firms but also generate positive spillover effects across markets by promoting efficient capital deployment and financial stability. These insights are particularly relevant for developed economies seeking sustained growth, improved corporate governance, and resilient financial systems.

detail.abstract: This report establishes the geometric foundations of the 2024–2026 macro‑financial transition and identifies the emergence of a Minsky Singularity—a structural regime in which market prices continue rising while the manifold of systemic risk collapses. Using the Universal Risk Framework (URF) and the Econosysmographe™, a seven‑series system is processed through 5×5 geometric operators to extract the intrinsic structure of systemic variance. The diagnostics reveal a Topological Survival Score (TSS) of 48.18%, below the 50% geometric bankruptcy threshold, a spectral entropy of 0.4094 indicating extreme concentration, and a Ricci curvature profile centered on PC1 and PC2 that confirms structural fatigue in the macro‑credit architecture. Together, these markers identify the terminal boundary of the growth regime as of January 2026. The report provides a geometric map of the transition, enabling institutions to detect structural exhaustion before it manifests in traditional indicators and forming the baseline for the expanded high‑dimensional monitoring systems deployed in MVP2.

title: Dominant Dynamics Equilibrium Model (DDEM)

detail.title: Dominant Dynamics Equilibrium Model (DDEM)
detail.abstract: Financial crises often emerge in environments that appear stable according to standard risk indicators, while similar shocks can produce radically different outcomes depending on underlying structural conditions. This paper introduces the Dominant Dynamics Equilibrium Model (DDEM), a dynamic mean-field framework designed to study systemic fragility, regime transitions, and crisis evolution through the lens of state-dependent dynamics. Rather than defining equilibrium as an optimal or efficient allocation, the DDEM interprets equilibrium as a configuration of dominant interacting dynamics-comprising leverage, liquidity, narratives, and delayed accounting recognition-that remains stable only in the absence of viable deviation paths. Within this framework, crises arise endogenously as transitions between dynamically dominant regimes, rather than as mechanical responses to large exogenous shocks. A central feature of the model is the explicit separation between fast-moving stress triggers and slow-moving latent fragility, allowing periods of apparent calm to coexist with the accumulation of structural vulnerability. Liquidity contraction, margin constraints, and forced deleveraging generate nonlinear amplification, while narrative-driven distortions of fundamentals accumulate through an overhang mechanism and are recognized only via delayed, discrete write-offs. Post-crisis dynamics are characterized by endogenous bifurcations, leading to qualitatively different outcomes such as recovery, stagnation, or persistent structural damage. These interacting mechanisms naturally define a multidimensional state space in which system configurations, regimes, and transitions can be represented geometrically. The DDEM is implemented as a dynamic simulation model, and its behavior is illustrated through representative trajectories and state-conditional projections in phase space across alternative parameter configurations. The reported results do not correspond to specific historical episodes, but instead illustrate structural possibilities implied by the system's dynamics and the geometry of its state space. By framing risk appetite as a region of phase space and crises as state-dependent regime transitions, the DDEM provides a conceptual complement to existing approaches to systemic risk. While not intended as a predictive or calibrated tool, the framework offers a coherent geometric grammar for understanding how systemic fragility accumulates, propagates, and resolves, and serves as a foundation for future extensions toward ensemble-based analyses.

title: Renewable Energy & the Global Energy Transition : Sectoral Outlook, Economics, Policy Frameworks, and Investment Implications (Global with an India Lens)

detail.title: Renewable Energy & the Global Energy Transition : Sectoral Outlook, Economics, Policy Frameworks, and Investment Implications (Global with an India Lens)
detail.abstract:
The global energy transition is increasingly driven by economic feasibility, capital allocation, and system integration rather than policy ambition. The cost of electricity for solar and wind energy has fallen significantly, making renewable energy the lowest-cost source of new power generation capacity in most large economies. However, as the share of renewables in the energy mix grows, the key barriers to further growth are increasingly moving from generation economics to grid infrastructure, storage solutions, market structures, and institutional capacity. This represents a shift from a capacity-driven phase to a system-constrained phase of the energy transition.

This paper analyzes the renewable energy sector through a global framework lens with a deep dive into the Indian context. It analyzes the structural drivers of the transition, the cost and scale dynamics of technology, and the role of transmission and storage infrastructure in ensuring system reliability and economic viability. The paper highlights the growing mismatch between the pace of decarbonization in the power sector and the pace of change in the overall energy system, with implications for capital efficiency and long-term system resilience.

Applying the framework to the Indian context, the results show that although the cost of renewable energy deployment is globally competitive, investment outcomes are highly sensitive to execution risks such as transmission availability, financial viability of distribution companies, land and permitting issues, and regulatory consistency. From an investment standpoint, the sector is increasingly displaying infrastructure-like characteristics, with value creation through integrated platforms with strong balance sheets, access to low-cost capital, and system capabilities. The paper argues that the success of the energy transition in the medium to long term will be less dependent on headline capacity additions and more on collective investments in grid infrastructure, storage solutions, institutional capacity, and disciplined capital allocation.

title: Banking on Politics: How County Partisan Identity Shapes Deposit Allocation
affiliations: and Texas A&M International University

detail.title: Banking on Politics: How County Partisan Identity Shapes Deposit Allocation
detail.abstract: We provide causal evidence that shifts in county-level partisan identity redirect bank deposits. Using FDIC branch-level data merged with presidential election outcomes from 2000 to 2024, we exploit Republican-to-Democratic county transitions in a difference-indifferences framework augmented by a regression discontinuity design at the partisan votemargin threshold. Branch deposits in transitioning counties increase by 3.6 percent relative to counties that remain Republican. Event-study estimates show no differential pre-trends and a gradual deposit response that builds over one to three years, consistent with belief updating rather than an immediate portfolio or income shock. The effect is concentrated among branches of the largest banks and is roughly three times larger in counties where survey-based measures of institutional trust fall below the national median. Placebo tests confirm that partisan transitions reshape the intensive margin of deposit allocation without altering the local supply of banking services. The evidence indicates that political identity influences one of the most basic household financial decisions, and through this channel, affects the geographic distribution of bank funding.

title: A Profession in Search of a Theory: Bridging the Research-Practice Divide to Establish Evidence-Based Planning for the Financial Planning Profession

detail.title: A Profession in Search of a Theory: Bridging the Research-Practice Divide to Establish Evidence-Based Planning for the Financial Planning Profession
detail.abstract:
The financial planning profession currently lacks a “unifying scientific theory,” relying instead on fragmented conceptual and “siloed” research from many professions that rarely coordinate except on the margins, and certainly not towards a fully integrated effort to unify towards any overall financial planning objective of “unified scientific theory” for the financial planning profession as a whole. This paper defines a unifying scientific theory as a broad, falsifiable explanation, arguing that current research is fragmented and fails to apply rigorous scientific methods, creating a persistent gap between academia and practice overall.

To mature the field, a paradigm shift toward an “Evidence-Based Planning (EBP)” system, analogous to Evidence-Based Medicine (EBM), is proposed. This requires addressing the disconnect among researchers, practitioners, and software developers/artificial intelligence, the latter who are posited as the critical linchpin for integrating testable research into practice.

Key deficiencies identified, as examples of non-use of scientific theory which includes the lack of robust “control variables”, siloed professions leads to lack of research sharing and application, and the failure to incorporate the “sequential effects of aging,” necessitating a move from static to dynamic, serially sequenced models. As an example of non-use of scientific principles, the paper proposes replacing the non-falsifiable planning metrics (e.g., “Probability of Failure (POF)” or “4% rule”) with the falsifiable control variables (e.g., simulation Iteration Failure Rates (IFR)).

Achieving a unified EBP system requires coordinated, multidisciplinary research and potential leadership from institutions like the CFP® Board of Standards, and many other professions’ leadership, to establish an empirically validated professional system seeking a unifying scientific theory for the whole of financial planning as a single profession made up of many disciplines that touch on personal finance.

detail.abstract: Heavy metal contamination of freshwater ecosystems poses a persistent environmental challenge because of the nonbiodegradable nature of metals, their bioaccumulation, and their adverse effects on aquatic biodiversity and human health. Microbial bioremediation has emerged as a sustainable and eco-friendly alternative to conventional physicochemical treatment methods. This review critically synthesizes recent advances in microbial bioremediation strategies for the detoxification of heavy metals in freshwater ecosystems, with an emphasis on microbial diversity, detoxification mechanisms, technological innovations, and field-scale applicability. A systematic evaluation of peer-reviewed literature revealed that diverse microbial taxa, including bacteria, fungi, algae, and engineered strains, exhibit substantial metal removal capabilities through mechanisms such as biosorption, bioaccumulation, biotransformation, and biomineralization. Compared with single-strain approaches, microbial consortia, biofilm-based systems, and synergistic plant–microbe interactions consistently demonstrate enhanced multimetal detoxification efficiency and improved environmental resilience. Advances in genetic engineering, synthetic biology, nanobioremediation, and continuous treatment systems have further strengthened microbial remediation potential. Despite promising laboratory-scale outcomes, the translation of microbial bioremediation to field applications remains constrained by genetic stability, biosafety concerns, environmental complexity, scalability, and regulatory limitations. This review highlights critical knowledge gaps, emphasizes the need for standardized performance metrics and long-term field validation, and advocates for interdisciplinary integration of biotechnology, ecology, and environmental engineering. Overall, this synthesis provides a comprehensive framework to guide future research and supports the development of effective, scalable, and environmentally compatible microbial bioremediation strategies for sustainable freshwater ecosystem restoration.

title: Experimental Performance Investigation of a Double-tube Heat Exchanger for Ground Coupled Air Conditioning System

detail.title: Experimental Performance Investigation of a Double-tube Heat Exchanger for Ground Coupled Air Conditioning System
detail.abstract: Growing energy demand for cooling has increased interest in alternative condenser designs that can deliver higher efficiency with reduced environmental impact. This work presents an experimental investigation of a double-tube heat exchanger (DTHX) integrated into a ground-coupled air-conditioning system. Unlike conventional air-cooled condensers, the DTHX employed groundwater as a cooling medium in a counter-flow arrangement with the refrigerant. Tests were conducted at water flow rates of 0.076 kg/s, 0.11 kg/s, and 0.145 kg/s, and under varying inlet water temperatures. The findings show that the DTHX consistently enhanced heat rejection and subcooling, leading to improved cooling capacity and coefficient of performance (COP). The maximum cooling capacity of 2.877 kW and COP of 2.96 were recorded at 0.145 kg/s, outperforming the conventional air-cooled condenser by nearly 28%. Moreover, system performance was strongly affected by inlet water temperature, with lower temperatures yielding notable efficiency gains. These results suggest that DTHXs can provide a reliable, compact, and sustainable alternative for high-efficiency air-conditioning systems in regions with accessible groundwater resources.

title: A Systematic Literature Review of Climate Econometrics Research
affiliations: University of California, Irvine, University of California, Irvine, University of California, Irvine, University of California, Irvine, , University of California, Irvine and University of California, Irvine

detail.title: A Systematic Literature Review of Climate Econometrics Research
detail.abstract: Over the last several years, research has increasingly used econometrics-style statistical models to investigate relationships between climate change and macroeconomic trends. Such work, on aggregate, has shaped both decision-making at the policy level and public perception of the risks related to climate change. In spite of the proliferation of this work, the field is missing a large-scale systematic literature review with the goals of synthesizing current methodological trends and identifying research gaps. Here, we analyze the methodology and results sections of 274 climate econometrics papers, identified via database search. Our findings demonstrate a heterogeneous range of proxy variables used to represent both climate change and economic development, as well as the use of a variety of statistical techniques and software systems. Our findings also suggest several new areas of focus for the field, including with regard to the representation of uncertainty, out-of-sample model evaluation, computation of historical and/or future impacts, and public availability of study materials to support reproducible research.

title: Skill Atrophy and AI Productivity Measurement
affiliations: and AWS

detail.title: Skill Atrophy and AI Productivity Measurement
detail.abstract: How should we measure the productivity effects of generative AI? Recent experimental studies document substantial short-run gains. We show theoretically that measuring the long-run effects of AI introduces two structural sources of bias when adoption affects skill formation over time. In a dynamic model where workers learn by doing, the effects of AI delegation depend on AI's pedagogical quality. When AI delegation slows learning by substituting for cognitive effort, two effects arise. First, as adoption spreads, non-users become a degraded counterfactual because mentorship, spillovers, and training environments deteriorate, causing cross-sectional estimates to overstate lifetime effects (spillover bias). Second, even within-worker comparisons are distorted: state-conditional productivity gains can diverge from path-based comparisons because current skill is endogenous to past AI use, lowering the outside option against which AI is evaluated (state-path divergence). These biases can reverse the sign of estimated productivity effects in high-adoption sectors. We characterize when decentralized adoption is inefficient and discuss identification strategies that recover the welfare-relevant counterfactual.

title: Losers with Passports: Travel as a Mask for Emptiness in Literature and Late Modern Life

detail.title: Losers with Passports: Travel as a Mask for Emptiness in Literature and Late Modern Life

declarations.ethicsApproval: This article is based exclusively on theoretical, historical, and sociological sources and does not involve human subjects or experimental data. No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently and received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines the cultural and psychological meaning of travel in late modern Western societies. It argues that contemporary mobility increasingly functions not as a form of discovery or intellectual expansion, but as a symbolic substitute for inner development and social belonging. Drawing on sociological theory, modern cultural analysis, and selected works of twentieth-century literature, the study interprets travel as a performance of status, identity, and visibility rather than as an experience of knowledge.

Revisiting the social type of the “lost generation,” the article contrasts earlier literary portrayals of displacement, exile, and existential searching with today’s consumer-driven culture of movement. The work proposes that travel has become a ritual of self-presentation that conceals rather than resolves the structural emptiness produced by inequality, cultural fragmentation, and the erosion of shared civic life.

By framing mobility as a sociological phenomenon rather than a lifestyle trend, the paper offers a theoretical diagnosis of how modern societies replace meaning with motion and authenticity with spectacle.

title: The Systemic Model of Distributed Economic Validation (MSVED): A Conceptual Framework for Economic Legitimacy in Complex Institutional Systems

detail.title: The Systemic Model of Distributed Economic Validation (MSVED): A Conceptual Framework for Economic Legitimacy in Complex Institutional Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest, financial or otherwise, that could have influenced the research presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research does not involve human subjects, personal data, experiments, or interventions requiring ethical approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently and did not receive any external funding from public or private entities.

detail.abstract:
Contemporary economies operate under a growing structural paradox: despite unprecedented advances in information systems, accounting standards, and supervisory capacity, it has become increasingly difficult to distinguish economically legitimate activity from formally compliant but economically incoherent transactional flows. This paradox does not stem from a lack of regulation or data, but from limitations in how economic validation is conceptually structured within complex institutional systems.

This paper introduces the Systemic Model of Distributed Economic Validation (MSVED) as a conceptual analytical framework that reconceptualizes economic validation not as an isolated or ex post control mechanism, but as a distributed, preventive, and coherence-based systemic process. Under the MSVED, economic legitimacy emerges from the consistency observed across multiple institutional validation nodes—including economic, accounting, financial, fiscal, and governance domains—rather than from compliance within any single domain.

The MSVED is not proposed as a behavioral theory, an equilibrium model, or a normative regulatory scheme. Instead, it operates as a complementary analytical layer that enables the assessment of economic legitimacy through systemic coherence in highly institutionalized and interdependent economic environments. This working paper establishes the foundational conceptual scope of the MSVED and outlines its implications for economic governance, systemic risk prevention, and institutional legitimacy.

title: How To Govern the Confidence Machine?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Regulation & Governance, volume 19, issue 3, 2025[10.1111/rego.70017]

detail.abstract: Emerging technologies pose many new challenges for regulation and governance on a global scale. With the advent of distributed communication networks like the Internet, and decentralised ledger technologies like blockchain, new platforms emerged disrupting existing power dynamics and bringing about new claims of sovereignty from the private sector. This special issue addresses a gap in the literature by focusing the discourse on the issue of trust and confidence in the digital realm. In particular, looking at the evolution of the web (from Web 1.0, to Web 2.0, and 3.0), this article analyses how every iteration reflects a different way of dealing with the problem of trust online, resulting in a different regulation and governance landscape. Technology is often regarded as a new lever of regulation, attempting at resolving the problem of 'trust' online, either through the introduction of a new trusted authority (Web 2.0) or through the introduction of technological guarantees that provide more assurance-or 'confidence'-in the way interactions can be operationalized (Web 3.0). Yet, each of these technologies also introduce new risks and governance costs, ultimately shifting the problem of trust in a new direction, rather than resolving it or removing the need for trust altogether. The main contribution of the articles in this special issue is providing a better understanding of the trust challenges faced and posed by emerging technologies, and demonstrating how they affect institutional governance-in both theory and practice-with a view to help policymakers find appropriate answers to these challenges.

title: Stability Through Transparency: How Honest Liquidity Information Eliminates Systemic Fragility

detail.title: Stability Through Transparency: How Honest Liquidity Information Eliminates Systemic Fragility
detail.abstract: Financial crises are information events. They occur when the perceived liquidity of a system is tested and found to be less than what participants believed. The bank run, the market crash, and the liquidity crisis are all manifestations of the same underlying phenomenon: a gap between the perception of exchangeability and its reality. This paper argues that this gap is not an accident or a failure of regulation but a structural feature of economies in which information about liquidity depends on human disclosure. It proposes a taxonomy of trust sources across three economic domains: personal trust in the physical economy, institutional trust in the hybrid economy, and architectural trust in the digital economy. In the physical economy, trust in information is bound to personal relationships and does not scale. In the hybrid economy, trust is delegated to institutions (banks, auditors, exchanges, regulators) that choose to disclose information selectively and periodically, creating structural opacity that makes the gap between perceived and actual liquidity inevitable. In the digital economy, as defined by on-chain systems operating through immutable smart contracts, information about liquidity is architecturally transparent: verifiable by anyone, at any time, without reliance on any intermediary's decision to disclose. The paper argues that this architectural transparency does not merely improve stability; it eliminates the mechanism by which systemic crises propagate. A bank run requires uncertainty about whether liquidity is sufficient. When liquidity states are continuously and immutably verifiable, the uncertainty that triggers cascading withdrawal does not arise. The paper connects this analysis to the three-domain framework and pool architecture introduced in Lechner (2026a) and the liquidity-value dynamics described in Lechner (2026b), and argues that the combination of honest liquidity labelling with architectural transparency constitutes a structural solution to systemic fragility that applies in principle across all economic domains but is implementable with full fidelity only in the digital economy.

detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of economic and non-economic factors on Nepal's inflationary dynamics. The economic factors are money supply, fiscal deficit, trade openness, the wholesale price index (WPI) of India, the output gap, and non-economic factors, are changes in the policy regime to Liberalization, and unusual circumstances. The study has used time-series data for the period 1975-2022 from Nepalese economy. To assess the impact of non-economic qualitative factors, dummy variables have been incorporated into the model. The Auto Regressive and Distributed Lagged (ARDL) approach has been applied to estimate the long-run and short-run relationship between inflation and selected determinants. The findings of the study report that the money supply, trade openness, change and the WPI of India have significant impact on inflation, however, the output gap, fiscal deficit, and unusual circumstances are not significant in this study. Since the inflation in Nepal is determined by internal, external, and even non-economic factors monetary policy is still essential to curb inflationary pressure in Nepal. In addition, domestic productive capacity should be promoted to develop an import substitution and trade diversification strategy by encouraging both domestic and foreign investment through sustained peace, security, political stability, and a conducive economic environment.

title: The Liquidity-Value Inversion: How the Digital Economy Reverses the Foundations of Monetary Theory

detail.title: The Liquidity-Value Inversion: How the Digital Economy Reverses the Foundations of Monetary Theory
detail.abstract: This paper identifies a fundamental inversion in how monetary dynamics operate in the digital economy compared to the physical economy. In the physical economy, an increase in the money supply reduces the value of each monetary unit: more money chasing the same goods produces inflation. Monetary theory from Hume through Mises to Friedman treats this as axiomatic. This paper argues that in the digital economy, where value is determined by exchangeability rather than by the properties of the underlying good, the opposite holds: increasing liquidity provision for a token increases the value of each unit by enhancing its exchangeability. This inversion has profound consequences for monetary policy, issuer incentives, and price formation. In the physical economy, the issuer of money has an inherent incentive to expand supply beyond what the economy requires, debasing the currency for short-term gain at the expense of holders. In the digital economy, the issuer's profit-maximising strategy aligns with sound monetary management: deepening liquidity increases token value, which maximises the margin between minting costs and market price. The paper further distinguishes between centralised exchanges (hybrid-economy infrastructure operating off-chain orderbooks) and decentralised exchanges (digital-economy infrastructure operating on-chain automated market makers), arguing that the DEX is the primary price-setting layer for digital-economy tokens, with CEX prices following via arbitrage. This distinction reveals that the meaningful measure of a token's market health is on-chain liquidity depth rather than trading volume, a metric that is transparent, verifiable, and immune to the wash trading that distorts hybrid-economy markets. The paper extends this analysis to explain how price convergence toward the physical spot price emerges without a peg mechanism, driven by minting economics that create natural gravitational forces toward the physical reference price. The paper builds on the three-domain framework and balance sheet identity introduced in Lechner (2026a) and positions its claims as pre-empirical predictions that will be testable once real-world asset tokens operating under these principles achieve meaningful market activity.

title: Sectional Economics: A Unified Framework for Heterogeneous Economic Outcomes
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Sectional Economics: A Unified Framework for Heterogeneous Economic Outcomes
detail.abstract:
This paper proposes sectional economics, a unifying framework for representing individual economic outcomes as the interaction between structural group conditions and individual differentiation. The central idea is that economic outcomes are constrained by section membership—such as income brackets, institutional categories, or health strata—and that individual variation operates relative to these constraints rather than independently of them. Formally, the framework decomposes any individual outcome into a sectional baseline and an individuality multiplier. The baseline captures average conditions within a defined section, while the multiplier captures relative individual performance within that section. This decomposition is exact, metric-agnostic, and does not rely on functional-form assumptions, regression residuals, or latent-variable estimation. The framework provides a disciplined way to analyze inequality, mobility, and policy trade-offs. It clarifies why aggregate improvements may coexist with persistent inequality, why exceptional individual success does not invalidate structural disadvantage, and why policies operate through distinct channels affecting baselines, section assignment, or within-section differentiation. Unlike standard approaches, sectional economics explicitly separates macro-level structural effects from micro-level individual variation without attributing unexplained residuals to noise.
The paper develops the conceptual foundations of the framework, formalizes its basic properties, outlines an empirical implementation strategy, and evaluates its consistency with established empirical regularities. Limitations and extensions are discussed to delineate scope and future research directions.

title: Digital Asset Economics: A Three-Domain Framework for Reserve Architecture, Price Formation, and Regulatory Design in Real-World Asset Tokens

detail.title: Digital Asset Economics: A Three-Domain Framework for Reserve Architecture, Price Formation, and Regulatory Design in Real-World Asset Tokens
detail.abstract: The prevailing approach to tokenising real-world assets treats digital tokens as representations of physical assets and inherits the constraints of the physical economy in doing so. This paper proposes a three-domain framework distinguishing between physical, hybrid, and digital economies, each operating under fundamentally different rules regarding value realisation, trust generation, and price formation. The framework rests on an empirical observation: the digital economy is messbar, nicht machbar, radically measurable and radically uncontrollable. Every transaction is recorded on an immutable ledger. No authority can compel adoption or engineer prices. This combination separates the digital economy from both the physical economy, where institutional friction enables policy intervention, and the hybrid economy, where digital technology is deployed within preserved institutional architecture. The descriptive elements of this framework, including the identification of exchangeability as the primary value driver, the liquidity-value inversion, and the trust taxonomy, are supported by already observable market dynamics. The architectural proposals that follow from the framework remain pre-empirical. The paper develops several interconnected contributions. Value in the digital economy is determined by exchangeability (Menger's Absatzfähigkeit), not by the properties of the underlying good, inverting the foundational relationship between liquidity and value per unit. Stability in real-world asset tokens is identity stability, the immutable relationship between token and unit, not price stability, resolving a category error in stablecoin classification. Price formation operates through market-driven convergence toward the physical spot price rather than a peg mechanism, with the convergence band reflecting digital-economy supply-demand conditions that a peg would suppress. Physical assets enter the digital economy through a balance sheet identity: the reserve and the token are bound as two expressions of the same balance sheet position, creating a bidirectional value relationship that enables in-ground commodity reserves to function as valid backing. Trust is architectural rather than institutional, and the honest labelling of liquidity states eliminates the structural precondition for cascading withdrawal. The framework reveals that current regulatory approaches focus on reserve composition (a hybrid-economy concern) rather than on liquidity architecture and information transparency (the digital-economy concerns that determine whether a token functions as claimed).

title: Frictional Macroeconomics: A Unified Framework for Real-Time Policy and Measurement
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Frictional Macroeconomics: A Unified Framework for Real-Time Policy and Measurement
detail.abstract: This paper presents a unified theoretical framework-Frictional Macroeconomics-that systematically incorporates four fundamental frictions shaping modern economies: (1) information frictions (rational inattention), (2) measurement frictions (lags and errors in official statistics), (3) financial frictions (balance sheet constraints), and (4) dynamic frictions (multi-scale economic cycles). The framework is microfounded from first principles and validated across 15 advanced economies (1960-2025) and U.S. Treasury auctions (2000-2025). Crucially, we distinguish between ex-post explanatory power (what happened) and real-time forecasting ability (what can be predicted), providing explicit bounds on each. The Generalized Phillips Curve with endogenous attention weights reduces ex-post measurement errors by 23.1% and ex-post GDP nowcasting errors by 27.9%, but we document that real-time forecasting improvements are more modest (10-15%) due to regime identification lags. We provide: (1) a methodology for real-time regime classification using only lagged information, (2) explicit parameter stability tests to guard against overfitting, and (3) bounds on expected performance degradation in true real-time applications. The framework provides operational tools while transparently acknowledging implementation challenges.

title: Why Did Ancient Egypt Stop Building Great Pyramids – The Evolution of a Tool of Power and Economy

detail.title: Why Did Ancient Egypt Stop Building Great Pyramids – The Evolution of a Tool of Power and Economy
detail.abstract: Why did they suddenly cease the construction of the largest Egyptian monuments, since these were so important to the pharaohs and had consumed enormous resources and time? Traditional answers – “they ran out of resources” or “religion changed” – do not fully explain the full scope and consequences of this phenomenon. The present theory elaborates and strengthens the validity of an earlier concept – both proposed by Jacek Krzysztoń – concerning the socio-economic function of the pyramids, showing that their eventual cessation was not due to failure or factors beyond the rulers’ control, but rather to the success of achieving the intended goal. The pyramids fulfilled their task: they integrated society, built the state, and jump-started its economy. Once that goal was achieved, the rulers did not rest on their laurels – they maintained the stability that had been attained and balanced the further development of the country by shifting to more flexible forms of public works projects, such as monumental temples. The author regards this change as a logical evolution of the tools of power and maintains the thesis that religion may have been a factor mobilising collective effort, rather than the primary reason for it. This reinterpretation shifts the emphasis from the afterlife to the here and now – and prompts a reconsideration of the role of the pyramids as a catalyst for the birth of the Egyptian state.

detail.abstract: This article introduces the first law of digital transformation: Technology changes quickly, but organizations change much more slowly. We argue that digital transformation is primarily a leadership challenge rather than a technical one, as human systems are significantly more complex to manage and change than technological systems. The paper outlines three key areas leaders must focus on to successfully transform their organizations: changing the vision, addressing legacy platforms, and improving organizational collaboration. Through examples from companies like DBS Bank, Asian Paints, Rio Tinto, and GE, the article demonstrates how effective leadership can turn digital transformation from a time-limited project into an enduring capability for continuous innovation.

detail.abstract:
Abstract

Since the outbreak of the armed conflict in Yemen in 2015, the country’s education system has experienced profound disruption, contributing to one of the most severe educational crises globally. Millions of children have been forced out of formal schooling due to damaged infrastructure, teacher shortages, displacement, and chronic underfunding. This paper examines the uncertain future of education in Yemen, with particular emphasis on the potential role of educational technology in mitigating learning loss and supporting educational continuity in conflict-affected contexts.

Drawing on recent reports from international organizations and empirical evidence from contemporary academic studies, the paper highlights the limitations of traditional classroom-based education under conditions of prolonged instability. It argues that technology-enhanced learning, when contextually adapted and pedagogically grounded, offers a viable complementary approach to sustaining education in fragile environments. Special attention is given to the use of inquiry-based digital tools, such as WebQuest-supported cognitive learning activities, which have demonstrated positive effects on students’ cognitive and spatial abilities within the Yemeni school context.

The paper discusses empirical findings indicating that low-cost digital interventions can improve learning outcomes in mathematics and related STEM fields, even in resource-constrained settings. Beyond immediate academic gains, such approaches contribute to the development of higher-order thinking, problem-solving skills, and conceptual understanding—competencies essential for long-term educational recovery.

The study concludes that rebuilding Yemen’s education system requires a dual strategy: restoring physical infrastructure while simultaneously investing in teacher training, curriculum adaptation, and accessible educational technologies. Evidence-based digital learning strategies represent a realistic and sustainable pathway toward educational resilience and future development in Yemen.

title: Promoting Financial Inclusion through Innovative Banking in Coastal Rural Communities

detail.title: Promoting Financial Inclusion through Innovative Banking in Coastal Rural Communities
detail.abstract:
This study evaluates how innovative banking strategies can promote financial inclusion in coastal rural communities. Financial exclusion remains a critical barrier to socioeconomic development in these areas, limiting access to credit, savings, and other essential financial services. A mixed-method approach was employed, combining case studies, literature review, and analysis of secondary data from Ghana and comparable regions to provide a comprehensive understanding of effective strategies. 
The findings indicate that ICT-based banking solutions, mobile money platforms, and strategic innovations in banking operations significantly enhance access to financial services. These interventions not only facilitate efficient financial transactions but also contribute to poverty reduction and broader community development (Annor, 2014; Joia & dos Santos, 2019; Jha, 2018). The study further highlights that tailored banking models that consider the unique socioeconomic characteristics of coastal rural communities yield higher adoption rates and long-term financial empowerment. 
The implications extend to both policymakers and banking institutions, emphasizing the need for supportive regulatory frameworks, investment in digital infrastructure, and community-focused financial literacy programs. Overall, strategic innovations in banking demonstrate substantial potential to transform financial inclusion, fostering economic resilience and sustainable development in marginalized coastal areas (Bongomin et al., 2018).

title: Your Company Doesn't Need a Digital Strategy

detail.title: Your Company Doesn't Need a Digital Strategy

detail.abstract: This article challenges the growing focus on "digital strategy" in business, arguing that companies should instead concentrate on developing better overall business strategies that are enabled by digital technologies. Westerman explains that technology itself doesn't provide value-rather, value comes from transforming business models and operations using technology as an enabler. Through case studies from various industries including paint manufacturing, banking, and shipbuilding, the article demonstrates how successful companies focus on strategic transformation rather than technology adoption. The author provides four key principles to avoid common pitfalls of technology-focused thinking and emphasizes that digital transformation should be viewed as an organizational capability rather than a project.

detail.abstract: This article examines how HR leaders and organizations are preparing their workforces for the impact of artificial intelligence (AI). The research reveals three proactive strategies some companies are employing: building general digital skills, predicting specific future job changes, and empowering workers to set their own career paths. The authors argue that while the timing and effects of AI on jobs remain uncertain, organizations should not wait to prepare their employees for a future where technology will increasingly transform work.

detail.abstract: Cyber disinformation is a global, very sophisticated phenomenon, capable of producing negative consequences on democratic values and institutions. This chapter argues that individual behavior of users plays a key role in the control of the phenomenon and aims to identify factors that impact on users’ behavioral intentions and cyber hygiene behavior. The research revealed the applicability of the Theory of Planned Behavior model and found that Moral Norms and Perceived Behavioral Control have an impact on Behavioral Intention and Cyber Hygiene Behavior. The findings of this chapter can provide stakeholders with important insights that can lead to improved responses to the phenomenon.

title: If Firms Go Digital, Do Humans Go Home? Exploring the E-Payment–Employment Tango

detail.abstract: This study explores the impact of electronic payment (e-payment) adoption on employment in Malaysia. Using firm-level data from the World Bank Enterprise Survey (WBES) 2024, this study investigates whether digital payment usage enhances or constrains employment. To obtain unbiased estimates due to the endogeneity, this study employs a Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS) approach, using internet availability as an instrumental variable. The findings show that higher e-payment adoption has a positive effect on employment, suggesting that digital financial integration supports business expansion and job creation rather than labour displacement. In addition, technology and firm age are found to positively influence employment, while firm size reveals heterogeneous effects, with large firms benefiting more than small firms. Overall, the results indicate that digitalisation, can promote inclusive and sustainable employment in Malaysia’s economy.

title: Taiwanese Disease, Formosan Flu: Central Bank as Information Gatekeeper

detail.title: Taiwanese Disease, Formosan Flu: Central Bank as Information Gatekeeper
detail.abstract: If an economy were a body and its policies were cells, then the rumoured “Formosan flu” afflicting Taiwan might be best diagnosed not with a stethoscope but with an information scanner. In The Economist’s recent cover story (which dubbed the situation “Taiwanese disease” or “Formosan flu”) it was the persistent undervaluation of the New Taiwan dollar that served as symptom and signal. The magazine’s use of its own Big Mac Index, an informal gauge of purchasing power parity that suggests Taiwan’s currency is around 55 % undervalued relative to the US dollar, turned what might seem like a quirky economic snack into a sprawling public health narrative of economic strain. But what if this isn’t simply about price mechanics or exchange rates? What if Taiwan’s central bank isn’t just a macroeconomic organ but an information gatekeeper, curating the very signals that shape how the domestic body hears itself, thinks about itself and behaves?

Taking in to consideration GenAI’s role in the spread of disinformation, the complex damages caused to people and the planet along with the proven negative effect to cognitive skills among users, this text advocates for critical perspectives, and ideally, critical refusal of GenAI.

title: Modern Consumer Contracting and Online Terms
