detail.title: Modern Consumer Contracting and Online Terms

keywords: Restatement of the Law of Consumer Contracts

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Missouri School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper No. 2026-12
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Missouri School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Company-crafted terms and conditions that supposedly govern modern consumer transactions are more lengthy, complex, and ubiquitous than ever before. Proliferation of online terms has been accompanied by increased judicial willingness to deem a contract duly formed based on passive and unknowing indicia of assent. Today’s consumer contracts are presumptively synonymous with a company’s online terms and conditions. Based on this framework, individuals cannot buy, join, stream, use, or access a myriad of goods and services unless they acquiesce to being legally bound to company-controlled terms.

Today’s “boilerplate terms” are electronic rather than printed, and this means that increasing their length, number, and complexity is costless. Contract formation outside of the digital sphere usually requires more time, more party engagement, and more active indicia of assent. But online contracting reduces transactional friction. The online context of today’s contracting rewards transactions that are streamlined and sped up. The fewer clicks and more auto-fill content, the less time to reconsider prior to commitment, and the greater volume of transactions – and a company’s profit. In cyberspace, people do not bother to find and read proffered terms, let alone attempt to negotiate them.

Consumers are therefore subject in contract law to lengthy and changeable digital terms authored and controlled exclusively by the companies with which the interact. If no one pauses to peruse a company’s standard terms, no one notices whether they include waivers of legal rights, and no one notices when those terms become longer, more restrictive, and more unfair. The length and complexity of terms disincentivizes even prudent consumers from examining them. No economic, market, legal, or reputational constraint limits the length – and, to some extent, content – of terms that are presented via hyperlink.

Not only are today’s standard contracts more extensive; they also impact people’s lives more extensively. The ubiquity of modern consumer contracts reflects technological and market developments, for example, the huge growth of e-commerce. Recent business model shifts from acquisition to access has led to a proliferation of licensing terms. People rely on subscriptions to be entertained, informed, in contact, and involved in various networks. Online terms and conditions now establish private rules that purport to govern everything from riding an electric bike to listening to a hit song. Because, increasingly, software and other services come bundled with various tangible goods, even in-person purchases of goods may subject a buyer to a company’s standard terms. Companies have embraced the potential advantages that come from unchecked power over applicable private law and carefully construct custom-designed legal frameworks and strategically channel their consumer counterparties into the relationships that are, allegedly, governed thereby.

Most courts today presume that a company’s standard terms make up the content of the parties’ contract. These terms are thus legally enforceable unless a court finds them so unfair and so shocking as to require judicial excision. But company-controlled content is not the equivalent of mutually chosen terms and treating them as such strains the theoretical underpinnings of contract law and raises concerns regarding abusive waivers of consumer rights.

Part I of this chapter briefly traces how modern contract law’s treatment of non-negotiable standard terms evolved from early skepticism regarding contracts of adhesion to the liberal formation approach taken by the 2022 American Law Institute’s Restatement of the Law of Consumer Contracts. Part II discusses the mismatch between contract theory and consumer contracting reality and articulates law and policy concerns associated with common types of boilerplate waivers. Current tensions regarding digital contract enforceability and emerging issues in law and technology related online contracting are discussed in Part III.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Research Technical Papers| Central Bank of Ireland

detail.abstract: We study the behavioural effects of Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL), a rapidly expanding form of consumer credit. Through an experiment conducted with a nationally representative sample in Ireland, we find that participants spend, on average, 4.39% more when using BNPL for purchases compared to debit cards. We demonstrate mental accounting effects where an inflated perception of available funds due to prior BNPL usage leads to a 22.2% higher likelihood of spending on a discretionary product. In parallel, we show the importance of anticipatory effects of such a credit innovation, whereby the mere expectation of future access to BNPL increases current debit card spending by 3.1%. While salient risk disclosures improve understanding of BNPL risks, they do not significantly affect usage or spending patterns. These findings highlight the dual psychological impact of BNPL on spending, support the rationale for consumer protection efforts, and establish the relevance of BNPL as a financial product of interest to macroeconomic policymakers.

title: Assessing the Macroeconomic Costs and Benefits of Borrower Based Measures

detail.title: Assessing the Macroeconomic Costs and Benefits of Borrower Based Measures

publicationDetails.detailsText: Research Technical Papers| Central Bank of Ireland

detail.abstract: We examine the costs and benefits of LTV and LTI borrower based measures (BBM) changes on future consumption growth rates. Costs are established using a semi-structural model of the Irish economy, which quantifies how macroprudential policy changes affect forecasts for expected consumption growth. Benefits appear in the form of changes to the tail risk to consumption growth, at the 5th percentile, over a forecast horizon of up to 4 years, given the same macroprudential policy change within a novel consumption at risk framework. We find that policy tightening actions involving LTV and LTI are associated with dampened central, or expected, consumption growth rates but appear broadly correlated with less adverse consumption growth tail risk. The timing of BBM adjustments is shown to be highly important, taking the phase of the financial cycle into account.

title: Bank Failures: The Roles of Solvency and Liquidity
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management

detail.title: Bank Failures: The Roles of Solvency and Liquidity
detail.abstract:
Bank failures can stem from runs on otherwise solvent banks or from losses that render banks insolvent, regardless of withdrawals. Disentangling the relative importance of liquidity and solvency in explaining bank failures is central to understanding financial crises and designing effective financial stability policies. This paper reviews evidence on the causes of bank failures. Bank failures---both with and without runs---are almost always related to poor fundamentals. Low recovery rates in failure suggest that most failed banks that experienced runs were likely fundamentally insolvent. Examiners' postmortem assessments also emphasize the primacy of poor asset quality and solvency problems. Before deposit insurance, runs commonly triggered the failure of insolvent banks. However, runs rarely caused the failure of strong banks, as such runs were typically resolved through other mechanisms, including interbank cooperation, equity injections, public signals of strength, or suspension of convertibility. We discuss the policy implications of these findings and outline directions for future research.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Macroprudential easing and mortgage borrower outcomes: Evidence from Ireland

detail.title: Macroprudential easing and mortgage borrower outcomes: Evidence from Ireland

detail.abstract: We examine key borrower level outcomes transmitted through Ireland's 2023 recalibration of the loan-to-income (LTI) limit for first-time buyers (FTBs), which increased the cap from 3.5 to 4. Employing identifying assumptions and propensity score matching on granular mortgage data, we compare the exposed FTBs (the treatment group) and second/subsequent buyers (SSBs, the control group) using a difference-indifferences design. Our findings show that the LTI easing led to an increase in credit for borrowers who were likely most affected by the limit, but this additional credit was used differently in Greater Dublin Area versus the Rest of the Country. Moreover, the LTI allowances (lending above the LTI limit) played an important role in facilitating access for lower-income borrowers before the easing, and we provide evidence that in the new framework, these borrowers are being facilitated credit as a result of the higher LTI limit, in line with the intended policy outcome.

title: Corporate Taxation in Open Economies

detail.title: Corporate Taxation in Open Economies

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the macroeconomic impact of corporate taxation. The analysis is conducted in a quantitative two-country model. First, the paper describes the long-run effects of corporate taxation. A reduction in the corporate-income tax rate increases GDP, wages, consumption, investment, and business density. The trade balance is at the same time negatively affected. Firms headquartered in a country which lowers its corporate tax become internationally less active and instead focus more on their domestic market. Next, the paper examines transitional dynamics that are induced by a corporate-tax reform. The short-run response of the economy can substantially differ from the long-run response. Finally, the paper investigates the effects of international profit shifting in high-tax and low-tax jurisdictions.

title: Quality Certification under Uncertainty: Theory and Evidence from Wine Competitions
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University - Carey Business School and

detail.title: Quality Certification under Uncertainty: Theory and Evidence from Wine Competitions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We have no personal or financial relationships with other people or organizations that may have influenced their study, or that could be perceived as having done so.

detail.abstract: Wine competitions act as quality certifiers for an experience good like wine, yet their heterogeneous rating protocols generate substantial uncertainty. We distinguish two sources: competition risk, arising from inconsistent practices across events, and rating risk, stemming from variation in jury assignments and score aggregation within competitions. We develop a discrete-choice model of a wine market with multiple quality certifiers and show that standardizing rating protocols Blackwell improves the information available to consumers and producers, reducing both risks and potentially improving welfare. We then propose a standardized rating system that normalizes judges' scores and groups wines into statistically significant quality classes, reducing rating risk. Using data from a wine competition, we show that our rating system reduces score variance and stabilizes award allocations. Standardizing rating protocols across competitions strengthens the credibility of ratings and enhances their welfare properties.

title: Conspiracy and Plus Factor Analysis
affiliations: and USC Gould School of Law

detail.title: Conspiracy and Plus Factor Analysis

publicationDetails.detailsText: U Iowa Legal Studies Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Iowa College of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Proving anticompetitive conspiracy from circumstantial evidence is maddeningly opaque. Courts marshal sprawling lists of plus factors—evidence like perceived action against self‑interest or opportunity to collude—yet rarely explain why any combination of factors supports the inference of conspiracy. Even a cursory review of recent opinions re-veals that the significance of plus factors oscillates wildly. The same evidence can flip from being treated as “pro‑conspiracy” in one opinion to “anti‑conspiracy” in another.

Our thesis is that confusion arises from evidence not being anchored to concrete, competing factual narratives. This is correctable. We pro-pose a competing narratives approach in which cases are resolved by explicitly constructing both a conspiracy narrative and a legal‑action narrative and then evaluating the comparative fit of each of these narratives to the available evidence. This test is internally consistent, economically grounded, and frees courts from the need to struggle with unworkable lists of plus factors.

Beyond resolving the paradox of how to reason about limited evidence of concealed conspiracies, our framework offers a template for reexamining other multifactor tests. By grounding circumstantial inference in the same comparative epistemology that evidence scholars already recommend as a model of factfinding, we show how unwieldy tests can be transformed into practical, court‑friendly tools for restoring confidence and predictability to law.

title: Differential Acceleration: United States-European Productivity Divergence in Technology-Intensive Sectors

detail.title: Differential Acceleration: United States-European Productivity Divergence in Technology-Intensive Sectors
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether productivity gains in the United States occur at the expense of productivity growth in Europe. Using sectoral labor productivity data from the European Union Productivity Accounts (EU KLEMS) and the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) for 2003-2023, inverse relationships between United States and European productivity dynamics are tested across nine industrial sectors. At the aggregate level, productivity exhibits strong positive co-movement. However, an acceleration framework using second differences reveals substantial sectoral heterogeneity. In technology-intensive sectors-Information and Communication, Professional Services, and Finance-the acceleration response coefficient equals 0.34, compared with 1.06 in traditional sectors, yielding a statistically significant interaction of-0.72 (p < 0.001). When productivity growth accelerates in United States technology sectors, European productivity growth accelerates considerably less. This pattern intensified after 2016. The results suggest that the widening transatlantic productivity gap reflects differential capacity to capture productivity gains from technological change.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Cognitive Finance: Investigating the Impact of AI Nudges on Financial Behaviour
affiliations: and

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Cognitive Finance: Investigating the Impact of AI Nudges on Financial Behaviour
detail.abstract: The explosion of financial technology (fintech) has revolutionized the way we manage our personal finances, allowing individuals to save, budget, spend, and invest through digital channels. Despite this progress, financial decision making is often affected by cognitive biases such as loss aversion, present bias, status quo bias and framing effects. We are all aware of the lack of saving, impulsive spending and poor investment choices that result from these biases. Nudging, originating from the field of behavioural economics, offers a toolkit that we can use to reduce such distortions by altering choice architecture. The advent of AI-driven nudges is a game changer, as artificial intelligence affords the capability for dynamic personalization, realtime adaptation, and scalable interventions that transcend conventional static nudges. This study aims to explore two goals: (1) to explore the effects of AI-powered nudges on saving, budgeting, spending, and investment behaviors and (2) to analyze the impact of AI enabled nudges in mitigating cognitive biases in financial decision-making. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional survey of 372 fintech users, including validated scales to measure nudges, reduction in cognitive biases and financial behaviours. The results of the Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) showed that the model fit was good and the correlation among constructs was high. Results indicate that AI-driven nudges had a significant positive impact on saving (v = 0.41), budgeting (v = 0.35), spending (v = 0.28) and investment (v = 0.33) behaviours (p < 0.001). Nudges also helped to lower cognitive biases (b = 0.52, p < 0.001) which in turn had a positive effect on financial behaviours (b = 0.39, p < 0.001). Mediational analysis confirmed a partial mediation with nudges having a direct and indirect effect on behaviours through bias reduction. The results feed into theory by tying together behavioural economics, cognitive finance and AI-driven personalisation. Pragmatically, they provide developers in the fintech sector with playbooks for how to build ethical nudges, regulators with how to impose transparency and users with how to build sustainable financial health. The study underscores the duality of AI powered nudges as tools of empowerment and ethical stewardship within the digital financial ecosystem.

title: When the Spare Tyre Goes Flat: Monetary Policy Transmission through Non-Banks
affiliations: and

detail.title: When the Spare Tyre Goes Flat: Monetary Policy Transmission through Non-Banks

publicationDetails.detailsText: Research Technical Papers| Central Bank of Ireland

detail.abstract: We examine how monetary policy transmits through non-bank lenders (NBLs) using comprehensive loan-level data covering the universe of all loans in an economy. A one-percentage-point (pp) increase in the policy rate leads NBLs to raise lending rates by 0.17 pp more than banks and to contract credit sharply on the extensive margin. We show that this amplification is driven by a liability wedge: banks’ price-insensitive deposit franchise stabilizes their funding costs, whereas NBLs rely on short-term wholesale debt that reprices immediately. This funding fragility exposes NBLs to rapid balance-sheet deterioration, resulting in higher pass-through and a stronger contraction in lending. This credit contraction spills over to the real economy, causing firms with high non-bank exposure to reduce assets, liabilities, employment, and profitability significantly more than bank-dependent firms. Consequently, we show that NBLs can act as stronger amplifiers of monetary policy than banks.

title: Minimum Wage Policy as a Migration Filter: Evidence on Low-Income Immigrant Size and Selection

detail.title: Minimum Wage Policy as a Migration Filter: Evidence on Low-Income Immigrant Size and Selection
detail.abstract:
This paper studies how minimum wage policy affects both the size and composition of low-income immigrant populations through migration and location choices. I develop a simple two-sector model with legal and illegal employment to show that, even under partial compliance, higher minimum wages raise the reservation wage required for migration. As a result, minimum wage increases reduce the scale of low-income immigration while improving average immigrant quality through selection at the margin.

I test these implications using U.S. data from the American Community Survey from 2005 to 2023. Empirically, I examine how state minimum wages are associated with immigrant population stocks and pre-migration wages across years since arrival. The results reveal pronounced lifecycle heterogeneity. Newly arrived immigrants are more likely to locate initially in high-minimum-wage states, but over time higher minimum wages are associated with reduced stocks of low-wage immigrants. Consistent with the model, immigrants who locate in higher-minimum-wage states are positively selected in terms of pre-migration earnings, particularly at the time of initial arrival. Selection effects are concentrated among newly arrived immigrants, while for long-tenured immigrants minimum wage increases primarily operate through preservation of existing stocks rather than changes in immigrant quality.

Together, these findings show that minimum wage policy-traditionally viewed as a domestic labor market institution-can function as an implicit migration filter, shaping who migrates and where immigrants settle without directly targeting immigration status.

title: Analysing Implied Volatility Smirk to Predict the US Stock Market Crash During the Global Financial Crisis
affiliations: Murdoch University - School of Business, Murdoch University and Murdoch University - School of Business

detail.title: Analysing Implied Volatility Smirk to Predict the US Stock Market Crash During the Global Financial Crisis

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Open Innovation: Technology, Market, and Complexity, volume 9, issue 4, 2023[10.1016/j.joitmc.2023.100165]

detail.abstract: This study analyses the presence of implied volatility smirk (IVS) and its predictability of the US stock market crash during the Global Financial Crisis (GFC) through the in-sample and out-of-sample tests. The in-sample investigation was conducted for 18 cases (cases 1-18) to confirm the development of IVS during GFC (2007-2009). It also examined another 18 cases (cases 19-36) to ensure the absence of the IVS in the post-GFC period (2010-2011). Finally, an out-of-sample test analysed 63 cases (cases 37-99) to assess the predictability of IVS for the stock market crash during the GFC. The study reveals several critical findings. The in-sample test results show the negative return from simultaneous trading of out-of-the-money put options (OTMP) and at-themoney call options (ATMC) due to out-of-the-money put options implied volatility (OTMPIV) is higher than atthe-money call options implied volatility (ATMCIV) for all 18 cases (cases 1-18), confirming the development of IVS during GFC. However, findings of the in-sample test for cases 19-36 reveal the positive return from simultaneous trading of OTMP and ATMC because of the lower value of OTMPIV compared to ATMCIV, ensuring no occurrence of IVS in the post-GFC period. Finally, only 13 out of 63 cases (from cases 37-99) under the out-ofsample test show the IVS can forecast negative returns in an abnormal stock market. Further, the predictability of IVS for the US stock market crash depends on the maturity of options, forecast horizon, and options trading period

title: Blockchain-Enabled Diminishing Musharakah Sukuk: A Shariah-Compliant Alternative to Conventional Leveraged Buyouts

detail.title: Blockchain-Enabled Diminishing Musharakah Sukuk: A Shariah-Compliant Alternative to Conventional Leveraged Buyouts
detail.abstract: Conventional leveraged buyouts rely on interest-bearing debt, which is prohibited under Islamic law, limiting Muslim investor participation in private equity markets. Existing Shariah-compliant alternatives face challenges such as illiquidity, high transaction costs, and limited scalability. This paper proposes a Blockchain-Enabled Diminishing Musharakah Sukuk (DMS) framework that integrates traditional Islamic contracts with tokenization, smart contracts, and decentralized oracles. The framework allows 70–80% leverage through asset-backed sukuk while maintaining profit-sharing mechanisms, targeting a 12–15% internal rate of return (IRR). Tokenization reduces minimum investments from $1–5 million to $10,000–50,000, and smart contract automation lowers administrative costs by 30–50%. Implementation pathways are analyzed through regulatory sandboxes in the UAE and Qatar. Key challenges include smart contract vulnerabilities, oracle manipulation risks, legal enforceability uncertainties, and scholarly acceptance of algorithmic execution. This framework provides private equity firms with access to $6 trillion in Islamic finance assets while promoting financial inclusion.

title: Temporary Rules (Report to the Administrative Conference of the United States)

detail.title: Temporary Rules (Report to the Administrative Conference of the United States)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This report was prepared for the consideration of the Administrative Conference of the United States. It does not necessarily reflect the views of the Conference (including its Council, committees, or members).

detail.abstract: Although agencies typically intend for rules to remain in effect indefinitely, they also issue temporary rules—which we define as legislative rules with a specific expiration date—to manage everything from Coast Guard security zones to multi-year pilot programs.  Despite their widespread use, temporary rules have rarely been studied comprehensively. This report examines the legal and procedural choices agencies face when issuing temporary rules, drawing on the legal history and APA requirements for temporary rulemaking, agency case studies, and a survey of statutory frameworks in all 50 states. It provides best practices for agencies when developing temporary rules and engaging with the public on them.

title: Toward Next-Generation Climate Modeling in India: Lessons and Pathways for Action
affiliations: , Council on Energy, Environment & Water (CEEW), affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Council on Energy, Environment & Water (CEEW), Council on Energy, Environment & Water (CEEW), Council on Energy, Environment & Water (CEEW), Council on Energy, Environment & Water (CEEW), Council on Energy, Environment & Water (CEEW), Council on Energy, Environment & Water (CEEW), Council on Energy, Environment & Water (CEEW), Council on Energy, Environment & Water (CEEW) and Council on Energy, Environment & Water (CEEW)

detail.title: Toward Next-Generation Climate Modeling in India: Lessons and Pathways for Action

declarations.funderStatement: Sequoia Climate Foundation

detail.abstract: National climate-energy models have achieved limited traction in Indian state planning despite decades of methodological advance. The prevailing explanation emphasizes communication failures: models are too technical, outputs too abstract. We argue instead that the gap is institutional. States prioritize investment requirements, employment generation, and fiscal feasibility, which conventional model outputs address only indirectly. Environment departments, the typical entry point for modeling exercises, hold regulatory mandates rather than planning authority. Model credibility depends on sustained coproduction with officials, not technical sophistication. The scope-2 emissions problem exemplifies this mismatch. Production-based accounting penalizes states hosting power plants while allowing electricity importers to report artificially low emissions, a methodological convention designed for national reporting that creates perverse incentives sub nationally. We propose a five-pillar framework for next-generation modeling: decentralized capacity, equity and development focus, political realism, institutionalized co-production, and alignment with fiscal processes. Institutional pathways include Finance Commission conditionalities, a national-state modeling consortium, and state-owned Measurement, Reporting & Verification systems. The analysis, while grounded in Indian experience, extends to federated and developing economies where subnational governments hold implementation authority but lack analytical infrastructure for long-term climate planning.

title: Iraqi Council of Representatives Elections 2025: An Empowerment-Oriented Analysis of Political Participation and Representation Using the Positive Statistics Methodology (Baghdad as a Case Study)
affiliations: Commission of Statistics and GIS

detail.title: Iraqi Council of Representatives Elections 2025: An Empowerment-Oriented Analysis of Political Participation and Representation Using the Positive Statistics Methodology (Baghdad as a Case Study)

detail.abstract: This study analyzes the final results of the 2025 Iraqi Council of Representatives elections in Baghdad Governorate through the lens of the Positive Statistics Methodology, a quantitative analytical framework that prioritizes measuring empowerment, coverage, and electoral achievement rather than relying solely on conventional descriptive indicators such as turnout rates or seat distribution. The study uses official data issued by the Independent High Electoral Commission (IHEC), which recorded 4,359,490 registered voters, 2,129,883 actual voters, 2,024,499 valid votes, and 105,384 invalid votes, with 71 parliamentary seats allocated to Baghdad. The analysis applies a set of Positive Statistics indicators, including the Positive Empowerment Index (PEI), the Positive Coverage Index (PCI), the Composite Positive Achievement Index (CPAI), and the Candidate Positive Mandate Index (CPMI). The results show that PEI reached 46.44%, PCI reached 97.72%—reflecting the proximity of turnout (48.86%) to the equilibrium reference point of 50%—and CPAI reached 72.08 out of 100. The study demonstrates the scientific value of an empowerment-oriented quantitative model for interpreting elections, enabling comparison, cumulative assessment, and supporting analysis of democratic maturity within the Iraqi context.

title: Bayesian Persuasion under Bias Management
affiliations: University of Southampton

detail.title: Bayesian Persuasion under Bias Management
detail.abstract: A principal delegates choice to an agent whose decision depends on both beliefs and tastes. The principal can steer the delegated decision using two costly instruments: (i) an information policy that determines a Bayes-plausible distribution of posteriors, and (ii) a bias-management policy that shifts the agent's effective taste. We study a binarystate, two-action, convex hull of two benchmark tastes specialization with posteriorseparable information costs. The analysis admits an inner-outer decomposition: optimal bias management is bang-bang (either no intervention or the minimal intervention needed to flip the agent's action), while the optimal information policy is characterized by concavification of an endogenous posterior value function that already incorporates optimal management and information costs. This structure clarifies how information acquisition and bias management interact; they can be complements, substitutes, or both depending on the primitives of the model. Information changes which posteriors are realized and hence where management is used; management reshapes the curvature and kinks of the posterior value function and hence the marginal value of information. The model delivers regime classifications for pooling vs. informativeness and for management at different posteriors within informative signals, and highlights how comparative statics can be monotone or non-monotone depending on how concavification contact points move with costs.

title: Securities Regulation's Liquidity Rationale
affiliations: University of California, Irvine School of Law

detail.title: Securities Regulation's Liquidity Rationale

keywords: Securities Regulation; issuer-disclosure law; securities-fraud law; insider-trading law; stock-market liquidity

publicationDetails.detailsText: UC Irvine School of Law Research Paper No. 2026-04
publicationDetails.journalName: University of California, Irvine School of Law & Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
New Deal-based securities regulation is far from free. In light of this reality, legal scholars have long focused on the extent to which the core aspects of this regulation (disclosure, fraud, and insider-trading law) generate benefits for society that justify their significant costs. As things stand today, when it comes to at least the regulation of the stock market, two main interconnected accounts of the considerable benefits of these laws have been offered by law-and-economics scholars. One focuses on price-accuracy effects (the “price-accuracy rationale”) and the other on liquidity effects (the “liquidity rationale”).

This Article argues that while the price-accuracy rationale has been the subject of many individual broad and deep works of robust legal scholarship (and clearly identifiable sets of the same), the liquidity rationale has been materially underexamined by legal scholars. This problem is revealed by the below identification of the existing articulation of the liquidity rationale and ensuing critique of that articulation. Taken together, this identification and critique provide a broad and deep review of the rationale that paves the way for improved scholarly and (often-required) lawmaker analysis of the net welfare effects of the core securities laws. The end result is thus the type of individual liquidity-rationale-specific work that has been missing from legal scholarship to date—one that also adds to what can now be seen as a clearly identifiable set of recent works with an increasing focus on securities law and liquidity.

title: Instruction vs. Infrastructure: Asymmetric Returns in the University Production Function
affiliations: Northern Illinois University

detail.title: Instruction vs. Infrastructure: Asymmetric Returns in the University Production Function
detail.abstract: Despite massive increases in funding, U.S. higher education degree output has stagnated-a paradox often attributed to external cost pressures like Baumol's cost disease. This paper tests an alternative hypothesis: that internal resource misallocation, specifically the accumulation of non-instructional liabilities, crowds out educational productivity. Using a panel of 40,300 institution-year observations, I estimate the university production function via a Fixed Effects Poisson (PPML) specification, adjusting all financial inputs using the Higher Education Price Index (HEPI). The results expose a stark asymmetry in productive returns: a 10% increase in instructional spending drives a 2.65% increase in degree production, whereas an equivalent increase in administrative liabilities yields a null result (β ≈-0.001). Heterogeneity analysis reveals that this inefficiency is driven by the public sector, where liability accumulation represents a pure deadweight loss. These findings are robust to state-specific time trends and placebo tests, suggesting that the "Amenities Arms Race" creates an administrative overhang that is uncorrelated with human capital production.

title: Say's Law Finds a Home: GBIR, the Consumption Ceiling, and the Hunt for Alpha

detail.title: Say's Law Finds a Home: GBIR, the Consumption Ceiling, and the Hunt for Alpha

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.funderStatement: no one

detail.abstract: The Generational Benchmark Inheritance Regime (GBIR) taxes inherited wealth that merely tracks the market (Beta) while exempting wealth generated through active value creation (Alpha). This paper analyzes the incentive and growth implications of this tax asymmetry. I show that the heir’s optimal allocation to Alpha-generating activity is strictly increasing in the benchmark tax rate (dα*/dτ > 0), even under neutral expectations about outperformance. A hard consumption ceiling—empirically binding above approximately $500 million—ensures that $10–12 trillion in dynastic wealth is structurally available for reallocation. Kahneman-Tversky loss aversion amplifies the behavioral response: the benchmark settlement is experienced as a certain loss, triggering prospect theory’s most potent bias. I formalize the growth consequences using a Romer (1990) endogenous growth specification, showing that GBIR produces a permanent increase in TFP growth (dg/dτ > 0), not merely a Solow-style level effect—though even under semi-endogenous assumptions (Jones, 1995), the cumulative GDP gains are large. The resulting capital reallocation addresses a chronic pattern of venture capital concentration: PitchBook-NVCA data show that materials science, industrial technology, and advanced manufacturing collectively receive less than 5% of U.S. venture dollars despite representing large opportunity sets with high marginal returns under standard concavity assumptions. I argue that GBIR revives a version of Say’s Law in the market for innovation: the structurally induced supply of non-consensus capital calls forth the investable proposals that the current funding environment suppresses.

title: Closing the Gaps: Comprehensive Anti-Abuse Provisions for the Generational Benchmark Inheritance Regime

detail.title: Closing the Gaps: Comprehensive Anti-Abuse Provisions for the Generational Benchmark Inheritance Regime

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: No one

detail.abstract: The Generational Benchmark Inheritance Regime (GBIR) distinguishes between passive market returns (Beta) and active value creation (Alpha) in wealth transfer taxation. This paper addresses the critical question of operational feasibility by cataloging twelve potential evasion strategies and proposing specific anti-abuse provisions to neutralize each. The edge cases span five categories: intra-family wealth leakage, trust and entity structures, spousal planning, asset manipulation, and cross-border arbitrage. Without comprehensive safeguards, the regime's estimated $295 billion annual revenue would collapse to $120-150 billion. We prioritize provisions into three tiers by revenue risk: Tier 1 (existential threats requiring statutory inclusion), Tier 2 (significant risks addressable through statute or regulations), and Tier 3 (moderate risks manageable through regulatory guidance). The paper demonstrates that the GBIR's discrete valuation windows avoid the administrative infeasibility that plagues continuous wealth taxation, and that the regime can achieve both substantial revenue collection and powerful incentives for productive capital deployment if properly fortified against abuse.

title: The systemic footprint: revisiting risk mitigation in long/short and 60/40 portfolios through network connectedness
affiliations: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, National and Kapodistrian University of Athens - School of Economics & Political Science and National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

detail.title: The systemic footprint: revisiting risk mitigation in long/short and 60/40 portfolios through network connectedness

publicationDetails.detailsText: Review of Derivatives Research, volume 29, issue 1, 2026[10.1007/s11147-025-09226-3]

detail.abstract: Amidst the ongoing financial turbulence, this study evaluates the performance of well-established long/short and 60/40 portfolios within a network of ETFs repre-senting different investment styles (S&P 500, value, growth, ESG, Sharia, high-dividend, momentum, high-beta, low-volatility, VIX futures). For this purpose, we undertake an in-depth analysis of volatility spillovers, utilizing sophisticated meth-odologies such as the time-varying parameter vector autoregressive (TVP-VAR), the extended joint connectedness, and R-squared measures. The sample period spans from December 1, 2015, to December 31, 2024, allowing for a comprehen-sive examination of the risk-mitigation contributions of long/short and 60/40 port-folios based on their neutrality within the broader market network. Under the TVP-VAR approach, both the long/short and 60/40 portfolios demonstrate resilience to market shocks, with the former exhibiting a stronger stabilizing effect. In contrast, the advanced methodological frameworks expose both portfolios as net volatility transmitters, thereby restricting their risk-reduction potential. A closer examination of their net dynamic behavior indicates that both portfolios display time-varying patterns in their ability to curtail risk. Thereby, our research shows that the risk-dampening gains of these portfolios are not inherent, but are conditional on specific market dynamics. This provides crucial insights for investors and policymakers, underscoring the importance of employing a multi-faceted, network-based analyti-cal approach to accurately assess systemic risk and refine asset allocation strategies

title: Rolling vs. Expanding Windows in Mean-Reversion Strategies: Evidence from Gold-Silver and Cross-Asset Validation

detail.title: Rolling vs. Expanding Windows in Mean-Reversion Strategies: Evidence from Gold-Silver and Cross-Asset Validation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. The research was conducted independently and without financial relationships that could be perceived as influencing the results.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Five of six macroeconomic regime rules fail to improve a commodity ratio mean-reversion strategy once the underlying signal is properly constructed. These are Federal Reserve hiking cycle vetoes, inflation expectations, quantitative easing, tightening overlays and a combined hiking-VIX rule. Using the gold-silver ratio (GSR) as a primary case study over 2000-2026, I show that the choice between rolling and expanding z-score windows produces a Sharpe ratio difference of approximately 0.6, larger than the effect of any regime overlay I tested. A systematic 72-combination parameter sweep confirms that rolling windows (5-10 years) consistently outperform expanding windows, quantifying the cost of a common implementation choice. I test all six regime rules using 10,000-iteration paired bootstrap tests; the single exception (VIX-based position sizing) achieves significance only when validated across five commodity ratio pairs with 350 pooled trades (p = 0.001). Cross-asset validation using silver's exact parameters on gold/copper, gold/oil, copper/oil, and silver/copper ratios with no re-optimisation confirms that the method generalizes beyond a single pair. These findings suggest that regime complexity in production trading systems may compensate for signal construction deficiencies rather than capturing genuine macro effects, and that cross-asset pooling provides a practical solution to the sample size constraints inherent in low-frequency strategies.

title: She Manages the Money – He Spends It: Income Management and the Spousal Expenditure Gap in Japan
affiliations: University of Trier and IAAEU - Trier University

detail.title: She Manages the Money – He Spends It: Income Management and the Spousal Expenditure Gap in Japan
detail.abstract: This article examines how household income management relates to expenditure allocation within married couples in Japan. While a large body of literature studies income and earnings disparities, little is known about how income management practices influence spending decisions. Using unique data from the Japan Panel Survey of Consumers (JPSC), we analyze traditional arrangements in which husbands transfer their entire income to their wives for management. We show that under Full Female Management, wives have a significantly lower personal expenditure share, challenging the view that financial management necessarily reflects greater bargaining power. Although life and marital satisfaction are not negatively affected, these women report more financial concerns.

title: On the Tax Morale Effects of Irregular Presidential Transitions
affiliations: and

detail.title: On the Tax Morale Effects of Irregular Presidential Transitions
detail.abstract: We study how irregular presidential transitions affect tax morale. Our analysis leverages administrative tax records and a difference-indifferences design exploiting geographic variation in electoral support for ousted Peruvian President Pedro Castillo. We find that tax revenues in pro-Castillo districts fell by up to 16% in the quarter following the impeachment. This decline coincides with a persistent drop in presidential approval, short-run reductions in trust in the police, and increased reports of racial discrimination following the repression of protests. Effects are absent during a routine left-to-right handover and persist after excluding protest districts, highlighting the distinctive consequences of democratic disruptions.

title: When Disasters Meet Democracy: How Climate Shocks Near Elections Shape Environmental Policy

detail.title: When Disasters Meet Democracy: How Climate Shocks Near Elections Shape Environmental Policy
detail.abstract: In most democracies, the timing of elections is fixed by law. Natural disasters, meanwhile, also follow a seasonal rhythm. These two predictable cycles jointly generate a stable, long-standing calendar distance between a country's election and disaster seasons. In some places, voters routinely go to the polls just after the months when floods, storms, or heatwaves are at their peak, meaning climate shocks are fresh in public memory each time they vote. In others, elections reliably fall far from disaster season, so environmental crises are rarely salient when citizens choose their leaders. Where existing research leans on the randomness of shocks to study short-term political reactions of voters, this project instead exploits their predictability. I examine whether this built-in, long-run exposure to climate-shock salience systematically shapes how political parties communicate, prioritize, and ultimately govern on environmental issues. I argue that the foreseeable salience might incentivize politicians to enact pro-environment policies, run on pro-climate agenda and generally foster greater support for climate action. Preliminary evidence shows that both disasters and elections are strongly seasonal. On average, 51% of a country's elections and 45% of the floods since 1950 have occurred in the modal month. Balance tests reveal no meaningful differences in obvious confounders between countries with different election-disaster alignments. Early results further suggest that nations whose elections consistently follow disaster season tend to perform better on environmental policy indices than those whose elections reliably precede it. This stable, institutionalized variation, rather than reliance on isolated shocks, opens a promising new window into the political economy of climate policy.

title: Residential electricity consumption during extreme price events across different contract types Working paper
affiliations: University of Oulu - Department of Economics, Accounting and Finance, Government of the Republic of Finland - Finnish Environment Institute, University of Oulu - Department of Economics, Accounting and Finance,  and Government of the Republic of Finland - Finnish Environment Institute

detail.title: Residential electricity consumption during extreme price events across different contract types Working paper
detail.abstract: This study investigates the hourly electricity consumption patterns of households under fixed-, hybrid-, and dynamic-price contracts during two extreme price events at both ends of the pricing spectrum. Households on dynamic-price contracts demonstrate strong demand responses, with consumption decreasing by 26.5% during extremely high-price event and increasing by 40% during extremely low-price event, relative to consumption at the average price level. Households on hybridand fixed-price contracts show no statistically significant reactions. Controlling for potential confounders indicates that the price responses of the dynamic-price contract customers is mostly attributed to the contract type. Additionally, we explore households' attitudes toward the functioning of electricity markets with a survey administered after the extreme price events. Dynamic-price contract customers viewed market functioning most favourably, whereas hybrid-price customers were the most sceptical. The findings help electricity retailers and transmission system operators anticipate residential electricity demand behaviour under large price fluctuations.

title: Estimating Resource Games with Nonlinear Dynamics
affiliations: and

detail.title: Estimating Resource Games with Nonlinear Dynamics
detail.abstract: Nonlinear dynamics, such as fish reproduction or disease transmission, are central to many resource models, and economic insights often hinge on these nonlinearities. In such settings, linearization is inadequate, and the presence of strategic interactions makes structural estimation challenging. We develop a tractable estimation method for a general class of these dynamic games using the Generalized Method of Moments (GMM). Our approach accommodates heterogeneous agents and nonlinear, interactive equations of motion. We derive sufficient conditions under which GMM estimation is feasible and establish consistency and asymptotic normality. We apply the method to a fishery game involving Japanese anchovy harvesting by China, Japan, and the Republic of Korea and estimate their strategic harvest responses to climate-induced shifts in ocean currents.

title: A Transition Plan for Global Governance during the Birth Pains of the Multipolar World: The Atlantic-Pacific Sustainability Partnership (APSP) of Middle Powers
affiliations: University of California, Davis - Department of Economics

detail.title: A Transition Plan for Global Governance during the Birth Pains of the Multipolar World: The Atlantic-Pacific Sustainability Partnership (APSP) of Middle Powers
detail.abstract:
The growth of China into an equal economic power to the US has produced the bipolar disorder of paranoia about triggering the Thucydides Trap.  As both superpowers envisaged co-existence in the nuclear age to take the form of a Yalta-type division of the world into spheres of influence, they are racing to expand their spheres of influence before the eventual negotiations to define the boundaries of these spheres and buffer zones.  This rush to regional consolidation is dismantling the international architecture to manage multilateral trade, contain contagious diseases, undertake peacekeeping, and protect the natural environment.

US-China tension is spiraling upward because the of the vicious cycle generated by the interaction of three kinds of US-China competition – geostrategic, technology and trade.  US and China could end this vicious cycle by decoupling geo-strategic competition from the others with an arms-control agreement and by decoupling technological and trade competition with a WTO agreement on unfair industrial policy practices. Unfortunately, the level of mutual trust is too low to enable successful negotiations on these two agreements.

The upward drift in US-China tension is increasing collateral damage on the rest of the world e.g. increased fragility in the supply chains and reduced benefits from trade restrictions on goods from countries in other spheres of influence along with sovereignty diminished by the leader of the sphere.  The best outcome for a country is to be nonpartisan and trade with every sphere of influence.  Neutrality, however, is not achieved through self-declaration but through recognition by the superpowers.  A country is more likely to be accorded neutral status if it is a member of a neutrality coalition that can project collective force that matches those of the superpowers.  As the superpowers would be vigilant in preventing the formation of this strong neutrality coalition in the first place, such a coalition has to be formed relatively quickly, which means that the number of founding members has to be small. Furthermore, to allay the concerns of the superpowers, this coalition must have members which have close ties with the US, and some members with good relations with China.

The Rest of the West (consisting of the 27 members of the European Union, UK, Canada, Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand) and ASEAN should form the Atlantic-Pacific Sustainability Partnership (APSP) to maintain multilateral free trade, uphold the United Nations principles of peace and human rights, and protect global ecosystems, with the rich APSP members assisting the development and green transformation of poor APSP members.  As the collective GDP of APSP will be significantly larger than that of USA and China in a decade from now, both superpowers would have an increasing incentive to join APSP to seek alliance against the other.  If one joins, the other would quickly follow in order to avoid inevitable defeat from self-isolation.  When this happens, APSP would have crowded out the US-China Cold War.

title: Sentiment, Investor Sophistication, and Asset Bubble
affiliations: University of Hong Kong (HKU), HKU Business School, Peking University HSBC Business School and Wuhan University - Economics and Management School

detail.title: Sentiment, Investor Sophistication, and Asset Bubble
detail.abstract: We examine the relationship between investor sophistication and performance in an asset bubble model with market sentiment. Sophisticated investors possess dual advantages over unsophisticated investors: information precision and information speed.  The precision advantage enhances sentiment’s role as a coordination device: when sentiment exceeds a threshold, sophisticated traders become more optimistic, hold bubble assets longer, and ultimately suffer greater losses. Their speed advantage induces divergent trading responses—sophisticated traders with pessimistic signals delay selling while those with optimistic signals accelerate selling—yielding a divestment pattern featuring both greater delay and concentrated selling activity. The belief divergence between sophisticated and unsophisticated traders is non-monotonic in sentiment, and sophisticated traders exhibit greater over-optimism when asset quality is high. Our model produces testable implications consistent with empirical evidence.

title: Finding Nemo, Abroad *

detail.title: Finding Nemo, Abroad *
detail.abstract: In recent years, international students have become an increasingly important source of both revenue and research workforce at universities in developed countries. Yet little is known about how this expansion of educational migration has shaped the direction of scientific research conducted at these institutions. To study this question, I exploit the staggered introduction of English-taught master's programs (ETMPs) in biological and agricultural science departments at highly ranked universities in non-Anglophone developed countries. By changing the language of instruction, these programs lower barriers to entry for a broad pool of international students whose primary language is English. I measure the geographic orientation of research by linking the plant and animal species studied in each publication to their native habitats, using newly assembled habitat-level data from the ecological sciences. The analysis reveals large effects on both the composition of researchers and the geographic relevance of research output, indicating that changes in who enters universities can substantially redirect what science they produce.

title: When Do Business Incentives Matter? Global Evidence on Stage-and Horizon-Dependent Income Effects

detail.title: When Do Business Incentives Matter? Global Evidence on Stage-and Horizon-Dependent Income Effects

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available secondary data and does not involve human participants or animal subjects. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates when business incentives matter for economic performance by combining a unified income-based development-stage classification (Poor, Emerging, Advanced) with short-run (annual), medium-run (5-year), and long-run (10-year) PanelOLS specifications for 161 countries over 2005-2023. Using this framework, the analysis uncovers strong stage-dependent and horizon-dependent heterogeneity in the effects of the Economic Freedom Index (EFI). Poor economies experience modest and short-lived gains from incentive reforms, reflecting structural and institutional constraints that prevent medium-or long-run accumulation. Emerging economies exhibit the largest and most robust responses: a one-standard-deviation improvement in EFI raises GDP per capita by +21.2% over five years and +31.7% over ten years, with the annualized impact peaking in the medium run and plateauing over longer horizons. Advanced economies show no measurable effects at any horizon, consistent with diminishing marginal returns near the institutional frontier. These findings align with theories of institutional-incentive complementarity, in which moderate institutional capacity magnifies the responsiveness of firms and investors to regulatory reforms. The results imply that business incentives are most effective when institutional foundations are sufficient but not yet saturated, offering clear guidance for reform sequencing and development-stage-specific policy design.

title: AI Is Capital, Not Software: A Framework for Understanding AI Value Creation

detail.title: AI Is Capital, Not Software: A Framework for Understanding AI Value Creation
detail.abstract: Most enterprise AI initiatives underperform not because of model limitations, but because organizations deploy AI as software when it behaves like capital. Software is a tool that enables human work. Capital is a productive asset that generates economic output. This paper argues that AI belongs in the second category-and that the distinction has significant implications for how firms invest, govern, and measure returns. The core constraint in modern enterprises is no longer data or computation, but human judgment: scarce, expensive, episodic, and difficult to scale. Prior technologies improved the efficiency of tools while leaving judgment as a human bottleneck. AI inverts this relationship. By embedding expert reasoning into closed decision-action-feedback loops, AI converts judgment into a scalable, reusable, continuously operating economic input-produced at near-zero marginal cost and improved through use. * The observations in this paper draw on the author's experience designing and deploying AI systems for enterprise technology spend optimization, where judgment-intensive decisions occur at high frequency and traditional software approaches consistently underperformed. The patterns described emerged from building systems that operate autonomously within bounded decision domains.

title: The Brittleness of Efficiency: A Platen-Villermaux Synthesis of Systemic Fragmentation
affiliations: School of Mathematics and Statistics, The University of Sydney

detail.title: The Brittleness of Efficiency: A Platen-Villermaux Synthesis of Systemic Fragmentation
detail.abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for modeling extreme systemic risk by integrating the Platen Growth Optimal Portfolio (GOP) with the Villermaux fragmentation kernel. Conventional Gaussian models and jump-diffusion processes frequently underestimate the magnitude of "Black Swan" events, as evidenced by the liquidity crises of 2008 and 2020. By treating the market not as a continuous uid, but as a brittle structure subject to physical shattering, it is demonstrated that systemic risk is an endogenous property of market sensitivity. This shattering process is formalized through Peter Scholze’s (2012) framework of Perfectoid Spaces, where the market’s transition into a crisis is modeled as a non-Archimedean "tilt" into a fragmented regime. Our simulation of a 150-firm index over 1,000 periods yields hyper-leptokurtic returns (Kurtosis approx 88.59) and significant negative skewness (-9.19), matching the empirical "shatter" signature of the March 2020 pandemic dip. These results suggest that diversification is an illusory defense against fragmentation shocks, which are synchronized by a systemic benchmark provider.

title: Organic fertilizer substitution reduces reactive nitrogen losses in China's upland crops: Crop-specific responses and management optimization
affiliations: Zhejiang University, Zhejiang University, Guangdong Polytechnic Normal University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Zhejiang University

detail.title: Organic fertilizer substitution reduces reactive nitrogen losses in China's upland crops: Crop-specific responses and management optimization
detail.abstract: CONTEXTUpland crops are vital for food security but significant sources of reactive nitrogen (Nr) losses. Organic fertilizer substitution (OFS) is a key mitigation strategy to reduce these losses, yet its effectiveness varies across crops and management conditions.OBJECTIVEThis study quantified the effects of OFS on Nr losses for China's main upland crops (wheat, maize, soybean), explored interactions among agricultural management practices (AMPs), and revealed crop-specific differences to optimize AMPs.METHODSWe combined meta-analysis and machine learning (SVR, RF, and XGBoost) using 778 observations from 103 studies across China. The best-performing model was used to predict the effects of OFS and to perform multi-objective optimization of N input rates using a comprehensive scoring function.RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONSCumulative effects showed that OFS increased yields (wheat: +6.1%, maize: +25.6%, soybean: +7.4%) while reducing N2O emissions (-30.6%, -23.5%, -30.4%) and N leaching (-28.3%, -30.3%, -38%). Subgroup analysis revealed crop-specific differences, likely due to soybean’s biological N fixation and varying N demand. RF performed best and was used for subsequent analysis. Based on the RF model, N input rate, organic fertilizer type, irrigation, and residue management were identified as the main factors influencing Nr losses. Management optimization suggested that compost was suitable for wheat and maize, while green manure performed better in soybean. Wheat and maize generally benefited from higher irrigation inputs than soybean, whereas straw return improved nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) cross all crops. The optimal N input rates were 130, 160, and 110 kg N ha-1 for wheat, maize, and soybean, respectively.SIGNIFICANCEThese findings highlight the importance of crop-specific OFS strategies and provide practical guidance for reducing Nr losses while maintaining upland crop productivity.

title: Measuring Housing Market Slack
affiliations: University of Wisconsin - Milwaukee

detail.title: Measuring Housing Market Slack
detail.abstract: This paper develops a framework to estimate U.S. housing market slack---the deviation of inventory from equilibrium levels needed for stability. We estimate a housing Phillips curve linking slack to house price growth, where slack is identified as the common cyclical component shared by existing and new home inventories. Results show a statistically significant inverse relationship between slack and price growth, with persistent negative slack since 2010 and extreme tightness during the pandemic. A shock to the estimated housing market slack generates substantial, lasting effects on house prices and rents, with rental impacts peaking 24 months after initial shocks.

title: Do Economic Crises Reorganize Work? Evidence on Skill Demand in the Post-Pandemic Era
affiliations: RWI - Leibniz Institute for Economic Research, RWI - Leibniz Institute for Economic Research, RWI - Leibniz Institute for Economic Research and RWI - Leibniz Institute for Economic Research

detail.title: Do Economic Crises Reorganize Work? Evidence on Skill Demand in the Post-Pandemic Era
detail.abstract: How do economic crises change firms’ skill demand through work organization? This paper studies the COVID-19 pandemic as a shock that constrained physical presence at work and forced firms to reorganize production. Using German online job vacancy data from 2017–2024, we estimate an event-study that exploits pre-pandemic differences in remote work feasibility across occupations within firms. We show that most crisisinduced changes in skill demand faded within a few years. But one notable exception applies to interactive skills: demand for communication- and coordination-related requirements increased in remote-feasible jobs and remained elevated after the pandemic faded, especially in business services and in industries with strong communication technology infrastructure. These patterns do not reflect automation, but instead point to a reorganization of work around hybrid coordination. Our results thus show that temporary shocks can trigger selective and enduring shifts in firms’ skill demand through evolving workplace organization.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the long-run macroeconomic effects of a Fiscal Rebalancing reform that shifts taxation from payroll to consumption under a balanced-budget constraint. Using a heterogeneousagent model calibrated to French data, we compare pre-and post-reform steady states. The reform increases both aggregate labor and capital, with a stronger impact on capital in the heterogeneousagent model than in its representative-agent counterpart. It also heightens wealth inequality, as a disproportionate share of the increase in aggregate wealth accrues to wealthier households. A welfare analysis that accounts for the transition dynamics reveals a positive average welfare effect overall, although high-wealth and, separately, low-productivity households experience welfare losses. The results are robust across alternative calibrations and model specifications.
